0.title: 2 Corinthians: Strength in Weakness
0.overview:
Second Corinthians is the most autobiographical of Paul's letters and, by many measures, the most emotionally raw document in the New Testament. Where Romans is a theological treatise and Galatians a polemical defence of the gospel, 2 Corinthians is a window into the interior life of an apostle under siege — attacked by opponents, misunderstood by the very church he founded, exhausted by suffering, and yet mysteriously sustained by a grace he cannot fully explain. It is the letter in which Paul most fully exposes the paradox at the heart of the Christian life: strength made perfect in weakness, treasure carried in jars of clay, life produced through death.

The letter was written from Macedonia, probably in AD 55–56, after a painful sequence of events: a “painful visit” to Corinth that went badly (2:1), a severe letter that followed (2:3–4; 7:8), anxiety about how the Corinthians would respond, and then the relief of Titus's report that most had repented (7:6–7). Paul writes in the aftermath of that partial reconciliation, addressing a church that has largely come back to him — but not entirely, since a group of opponents (often called the “super-apostles” or “false apostles”) still commands a following and challenges his authority.

How many letters did Paul write to Corinth? At least four. An early letter, now lost, warned against associating with the sexually immoral (1 Cor 5:9); then came 1 Corinthians; then a painful visit (2:1); then a letter written with many tears (2:4; 7:8); and then this one. Many scholars think chapters 10–13 are part of that tearful letter, or a later one, because the tone changes so sharply at chapter 10. But no manuscript ever divides the letter; the tearful letter was written to grieve them over an offence, which chapters 10–13 never mention; and the change of tone is explained by Paul turning from the repentant majority (chapters 1–9) to the false apostles still at work. The more likely reading is that 2 Corinthians is one letter, and the tearful letter is lost.

The letter falls into three broad movements. Chapters 1–7 address the ministry of suffering and reconciliation: Paul defends the authenticity of his apostleship by pointing to suffering as its credential, not its disqualification, and unfolds a breathtaking theology of the new covenant ministry. Chapters 8–9 address the collection for the Jerusalem church — a sustained theology of generosity rooted in the self-giving of Christ. Chapters 10–13, which contain the “fool's speech,” are Paul's sharp and ironic defence of his apostleship against the super-apostles, climaxing in the account of his thorn in the flesh and the word that defines the entire letter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”

The letter's central theological contribution is its theology of weakness and glory. Paul's opponents measured apostleship by rhetorical skill, impressive presence, and spiritual fireworks. Paul measures it by the cross: authentic ministry looks like dying and rising, like carrying in the body the death of Jesus so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested. This is not merely Paul's personal psychological coping; it is a fundamental claim about how the kingdom of God advances — through the cruciform shape of those who carry it.

1.title: The God of All Comfort and the Yes of Christ
1.overview:
Some background makes this letter far clearer. Corinth was a rich, proud, commercial city on the isthmus between mainland Greece and the Peloponnese, refounded by Julius Caesar as a Roman colony in 44 BC and full of ambitious freedmen on the way up. Status, eloquence and success mattered enormously there. Paul founded the church around AD 50 (Acts 18) and later wrote 1 Corinthians. Things went badly afterwards: he made a short “painful visit” in which someone in the church publicly opposed him (2:1–5), then wrote a severe letter “with many tears” (2:4), and changed his plan to visit again. Meanwhile visiting preachers, impressive speakers with letters of recommendation, were telling the church that Paul was weak, unreliable and second-rate. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s reply, written from Macedonia once Titus brought news that most of the church had repented (7:5–7).

Chapter 1 sets the theme of the whole letter: God’s power shows up in weakness. Paul begins by blessing the God of all comfort, who comforted him in an affliction so crushing he despaired of life, so that he can comfort others and learn to rely on God who raises the dead. Then he answers the charge that his changed travel plans prove he is fickle. His message is not “Yes and No”, because in Christ every promise of God is “Yes”; God has anointed and sealed his people with the Spirit as a down payment. He stayed away to spare them, not because he wants to lord it over their faith.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The God of All Comfort
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul opens by naming himself an apostle by God’s will, the very point his critics dispute. Then, instead of complaining about a terrible year, he praises God as the Father who shows compassion and gives strength in every kind of trouble. The comfort he receives is not for himself alone: it equips him to strengthen others in their troubles. His sufferings and the Corinthians’ are bound together, and so is the comfort. He tells them frankly that in Asia he was crushed beyond endurance and expected to die, and he sees the purpose: to stop relying on himself and rely on the God who raises the dead. That God rescued him and will do so again, helped by their prayers, so that many will give thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
The phrase “Father of mercies and God of all comfort” (v. 3) is a carefully constructed title. “Mercies” is plural, and it echoes the Hebrew word for the deep, gut-level compassion that is related to the word for womb. “Comfort” shares its root with the name Jesus gives the Holy Spirit, the Helper (John 14:16). God himself, through the Spirit he sends, is the source and supply of all genuine comfort. No human comfort is ultimate; all genuine comfort is God’s own comfort mediated through creaturely means.

The suffering-comfort dynamic in vv. 4–7 is the pastoral theology of the cross applied to ministry. The wound is the credential. Those who have been comforted in their own affliction have something to give that those who have only known ease cannot supply. This is not a glorification of suffering for its own sake but a recognition that God wastes nothing — not even the darkest experiences of his servants.
verseByVerse.examples:
A pastor who has gone through a severe depressive episode returns to ministry and finds that his counselling of those suffering from depression has taken on a different quality. He is not simply applying techniques; he is giving what he has received. His people sense it. This is the dynamic Paul describes — not therapeutic expertise but the transferable comfort of one who has been there and been comforted by the God who is there.

And v. 11 puts the same dynamic in reverse. A member of the congregation who has never taught, never led and never travelled prays through the week for a missionary she has met once. Paul’s sentence says that her praying is not a gesture of support alongside the real work; it is a shoulder genuinely under the load. Churches that publish requests and never report the outcomes rob such people of the best half of it — the thanksgiving that Paul says was the point of the rescue in the first place.

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians is Paul’s most personal letter. Since 1 Corinthians, his relationship with the church had been through a crisis: a painful visit, a severe letter, an attack on his authority by some in Corinth, and later the arrival of rival teachers whom he calls super-apostles. Now, having heard from Titus that most of the church has repented, he writes with relief, love and warning. The whole letter answers one question: what does true Christian ministry look like? Paul’s answer is that it looks like the cross: strength in weakness, comfort in suffering, glory in jars of clay. Chapter 1 begins with a blessing of the God of all comfort, who comforts Paul in his afflictions so that he can comfort others, and who delivered him from a deadly peril in Asia to teach him to rely on the God who raises the dead (vv. 3–11). Then Paul defends himself against the charge of being fickle for changing his travel plans: his word is reliable because the God he preaches is faithful, and all God’s promises find their Yes in Christ. God has anointed, sealed and given his Spirit as a guarantee. Paul changed plans not from weakness but to spare them pain (vv. 12–24).

Setting and background. Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, about a year after 1 Corinthians. The events in between, pieced together from the letter: Paul made a second, painful visit to Corinth (2:1; 13:2), where someone attacked him publicly (2:5–8; 7:12). He then wrote a severe, tearful letter (2:3–4; 7:8), now lost, sent by Titus. Anxious, he left Ephesus after the riot there, waited for Titus in Troas, then went on to Macedonia, where Titus finally met him with good news (2:12–13; 7:5–7). Chapters 10–13 deal with false apostles who had arrived in Corinth.

Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God. Key words. His authority, which was being questioned, rests on God’s will, not human appointment.

And Timothy our brother. Key words. Timothy had visited Corinth (1 Corinthians 4:17; 16:10) and was now with Paul.

To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia. Key words. The letter was meant for all believers in the province, including Cenchreae (Romans 16:1) and Athens.

Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. Paul’s greeting: God’s free favour and the wholeness it brings, from the Father and the Son together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is writing to a perfect church. He writes to a church still struggling, and still the church of God.

In a sentence. From Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God’s will, and our brother Timothy, to God’s church in Corinth and all his people throughout Achaia: grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Relationships in the church can go through painful seasons. Keep working toward reconciliation, as Paul did.
verseByVerse.note: Paul wrote this letter from Macedonia, probably around AD 55–56, after a painful visit to Corinth and a severe letter written “with many tears.” Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. “Blessed” (eulogētos, praised): a Jewish form of praise (Ephesians 1:3; 1 Peter 1:3). Paul begins not with complaint but with worship.

The Father of mercies. Key words. A Hebrew way of saying the merciful Father, the source of all compassion (oiktirmoi, pity, tender mercy; Psalm 103:13).

And God of all comfort. Key words. “Comfort” (paraklēsis): encouragement, strengthening, consolation. The word or its verb appears ten times in verses 3–7. It is related to Paraklētos, the Comforter, the Holy Spirit (John 14:16). All comfort ultimately comes from God (Isaiah 40:1; 51:12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God removes all suffering. It means he comforts us in it.

In a sentence. Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father who is full of compassion and the God from whom all comfort comes,

For worship. Whatever you are facing, begin with praise: blessed be the God of all comfort.

parallels.desc: I, I am he who comforts you

verseByVerse.quote: who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.

Who comforts us in all our affliction. Key words. “Affliction” (thlipsis, pressure, crushing). In all: not some. God comforts in every trial. Notice: in affliction, not by removing it.

So that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction. Key words. God’s comfort has a purpose beyond us. We receive comfort in order to pass it on. Suffering trains us to help others.

With the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God. Key words. We give what we have received. The comfort is not our own wisdom, but God’s comfort passed through us.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only those who have suffered the exact same thing can comfort others. It means God’s comfort in any trial equips us for any trial.

In a sentence. who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort others in any trouble with the same comfort God has given us.

On a Tuesday. Think of a hard season God brought you through. Who around you is going through something similar? Comfort them this week.

parallels.desc: as one whom his mother comforts

verseByVerse.quote: For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.

For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings. Key words. Literally, the sufferings of Christ overflow to us. Believers, united to Christ, share in the kind of suffering he endured: rejection, persecution, hardship for the gospel (Philippians 3:10; Colossians 1:24; 1 Peter 4:13).

So through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too. Key words. As suffering overflows, so comfort overflows. Through Christ, by his Spirit, comfort matches and exceeds suffering.

What it does not mean. It does not mean our sufferings add to Christ’s atoning work. That was finished once for all (Hebrews 10:14). It means we share in the pattern of his sufferings as his followers.

In a sentence. For just as Christ’s sufferings spill over into our lives, so through Christ our comfort spills over too.

For worship. In your suffering, you are sharing in Christ’s. Ask him for his overflowing comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.

If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation. Key words. Paul’s sufferings were not wasted; they served the Corinthians. His suffering brought them the gospel and showed them how to endure.

And if we are comforted, it is for your comfort. Key words. When God comforts Paul, the comfort passes to them.

Which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer. Key words. “Patiently endure” (hypomonē, steadfast endurance). Comfort is experienced in endurance, not escape.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s suffering saves them. Christ’s suffering saves. Paul’s suffering serves their salvation as he brings them the gospel.

In a sentence. If we are in trouble, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which helps you endure the same sufferings we go through.

On a Tuesday. Your suffering, borne in faith, can strengthen others. Do not waste it.

verseByVerse.quote: Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.

Our hope for you is unshaken. Key words. “Unshaken” (bebaios, firm, secure). Despite the troubles of recent months, Paul is confident about them.

For we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort. Key words. “Share” (koinōnoi, partners). Partnership in suffering means partnership in comfort. They go together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering will end soon. It means comfort will come with it.

In a sentence. Our hope for you stands firm, because we know that just as you share our sufferings, you also share our comfort.

For worship. Thank God for the partnership of believers in suffering and comfort. Pray for a suffering brother or sister.

verseByVerse.quote: For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.

For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. Key words. Paul does not say what the danger in Asia was; it may have been the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23–41), a severe illness, imprisonment, or a plot against his life. Asia is the Roman province around Ephesus.

For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength. Key words. “Burdened” (bareō, weighed down, crushed). “Beyond our strength” (hyper dynamin). Paul admits he was overwhelmed. God gave him more than he could handle in his own strength.

That we despaired of life itself. Key words. “Despaired” (exaporeomai, utterly at a loss). He thought he would die. The great apostle was honest about his despair.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul lost his faith. It means he lost hope in himself. And it does not contradict 1 Corinthians 10:13, which is about temptation to sin, not the weight of suffering.

In a sentence. We want you to know, brothers and sisters, about the troubles we went through in Asia. We were under such crushing pressure, far beyond what we could bear, that we gave up hope of surviving.

On a Tuesday. If you feel crushed beyond your strength, you are not a failed Christian. Paul felt that too. Be honest with God about it.
verseByVerse.note: Paul does not say what the danger in Asia was; it may have been the riot at Ephesus, severe illness or another threat.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.

Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. Key words. “Sentence” (apokrima, verdict, official decision). Paul felt as if a death sentence had been passed.

But that was to make us rely not on ourselves. Key words. God’s purpose in the crisis: to strip away self-reliance. Even an apostle can drift into trusting his own strength.

But on God who raises the dead. Key words. The God who raised Jesus (and will raise us, 1 Corinthians 15) is able to deliver from any danger, even death. Abraham trusted the same God (Romans 4:17; Hebrews 11:19). When we have nothing left, we discover God is enough.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God causes suffering carelessly. It means he uses it purposefully.

In a sentence. In fact, in our hearts we felt we were under a death sentence. But this happened so that we would stop trusting ourselves and trust God, who raises the dead.

For worship. Where are you relying on yourself? Hand it to the God who raises the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.

He delivered us from such a deadly peril. Key words. Past: God rescued him.

And he will deliver us. Key words. Future: God will rescue him in future dangers.

On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again. Key words. Paul’s hope rests on God, not on circumstances. Past deliverance builds hope for the future. Ultimately God will deliver from death itself, by resurrection (2 Timothy 4:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul would never die. He was eventually martyred. But even then God delivered him, into his presence and to resurrection.

In a sentence. He rescued us from mortal danger, and he will rescue us again. We have set our hope on him to keep on rescuing us.

On a Tuesday. Remember a time God rescued you. Let it give you hope for what you face now.

verseByVerse.quote: You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.

You also must help us by prayer. Key words. “Help” (synypourgeō, work together with, join in helping). Prayer is real work, partnership in ministry. God’s deliverance comes in answer to his people’s prayers.

So that many will give thanks on our behalf. Key words. When prayer is answered, those who prayed give thanks. Prayer leads to thanksgiving, which glorifies God.

For the blessing granted us through the prayers of many. Key words. “Blessing” (charisma, gift of grace). God gives in answer to many people’s prayers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God is reluctant until enough people pray. It means God has chosen to work through the prayers of his people.

In a sentence. And you help us by praying for us. Then many will thank God for the gracious answer he gives to the prayers of many.

For worship. Pray today for a missionary or pastor in danger or difficulty. Then thank God when you hear how he answers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–24 — The Yes of God in Christ and Paul’s Changed Plans
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul defends his integrity. His conscience is clear: he has dealt with them openly and sincerely, by God’s grace rather than clever technique, and his letters mean what they say. His critics say his changed travel plans prove he is unreliable. Paul answers by pointing to God’s faithfulness: the message he preached was not a mixture of yes and no, because every promise God has made is confirmed in Christ, and the church says its Amen to that. It is God who keeps them firm, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a first instalment. Paul stayed away to spare them a painful confrontation, not to dominate them; he wants to serve their joy.
verseByVerse.theology:
“All the promises of God find their Yes in him” (v. 20) — This is the hermeneutical key to the entire OT: every promise — to Abraham, to Moses, to David, through the prophets — is fulfilled in Christ. This does not mean every OT text is directly about Jesus; it means the entire trajectory of divine promise reaches its destination in him. The “Amen” that believers add in worship is their ratification of what God has already declared: yes, it is so, in Christ.

The Trinitarian shape of vv. 21–22 is worth noting: God establishes (the Father), anointed (chrisas — sharing the root with Christos), and sealed with the Spirit, giving the Spirit as a deposit (arrabōn — the down payment guaranteeing the full inheritance, as in Eph. 1:14). The three persons are active together in the believer’s assurance.
verseByVerse.examples: A church member accuses her pastor of inconsistency when he changes a ministry plan he had announced. He is tempted to defend himself by cataloguing the reasons. This passage suggests a different approach: the goal is not to vindicate the decision but to demonstrate that the change came from genuine care for those affected — the same reason Paul stayed away from Corinth. Integrity is not the absence of changed plans; it is the transparent, godly motivation behind all decisions, including the changes.

verseByVerse.quote: For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand— just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you. For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.

For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience. Key words. Paul begins his self-defence. His conscience is clear.

That we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity. Key words. “Simplicity” (haplotēs, singleness of heart; some manuscripts read holiness, as the ESV notes). “Sincerity” (eilikrineia, purity, transparency). No hidden agendas.

Not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God. Key words. Not by worldly cleverness, manipulation or self-interest, but by God’s grace.

And supremely so toward you. Key words. Especially in his dealings with the Corinthians.

For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand. Key words. Some accused Paul of hidden meanings in his letters. He says: what you read is what I mean.

And I hope you will fully understand—just as you did partially understand us. Key words. They understood him partly; he hopes they will understand fully.

That on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you. Key words. On the last day, Paul and the Corinthians will rejoice in each other as the fruit of God’s work (Philippians 2:16; 1 Thessalonians 2:19–20).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sinless. It means he had been honest and sincere in his ministry to them.

In a sentence. This is what we take pride in: our conscience tells us that we have lived in the world, and especially toward you, with integrity and God-given sincerity, relying not on worldly wisdom but on God’s grace. We write nothing you cannot read and understand. And Paul hopes that, as you have understood us in part, you will come to understand fully that on the day of the Lord Jesus you will be proud of us just as we will be proud of you.

On a Tuesday. Can you say with Paul that your conscience is clear in your dealings? If not, put it right today.

verseByVerse.quote: Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace. I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?

Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first. Key words. Paul had changed his travel plans, and some at Corinth accused him of being unreliable. His original plan (1 Corinthians 16:5) had changed to a double visit, and then changed again.

So that you might have a second experience of grace. Key words. Literally, a second grace or benefit: two visits instead of one.

I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea. Key words. The plan: Corinth, Macedonia, Corinth again, then Judea with the collection.

Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Key words. “Vacillating” (elaphria, lightness, fickleness). Did I make plans carelessly?

Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time? Key words. According to the flesh: for selfish reasons, to suit myself. Saying yes and no at once: telling people what they want to hear, with no real commitment.

What it does not mean. It does not mean changing plans is always wrong. Paul changed his plans for good reasons (v. 23).

In a sentence. Because Paul was confident of this, he planned to visit you first so that you might be blessed twice: once on his way to Macedonia and again on his way back, so that you could send him on to Judea. Was he fickle when he planned this? Does he make plans in a worldly way, saying yes and no in the same breath?

For worship. Ask God to make you a person whose word can be trusted.
verseByVerse.note: Paul had changed his travel plans, and some at Corinth accused him of being unreliable.

verseByVerse.quote: As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.

As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No. Key words. An oath. Paul’s word, especially his preaching, has been reliable, because the God behind it is faithful.

For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I. Key words. Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth (Acts 18:5). The message they preached was Christ himself.

Was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes. Key words. Christ is not uncertain or contradictory. He is God’s definitive Yes.

For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. Key words. Every promise God made in the Old Testament, to Abraham, David, the prophets, is confirmed and fulfilled in Christ. He is the Yes to every promise.

That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory. Key words. “Amen” means “so be it,” and was said in worship to affirm what God has said. Through Christ, believers say Amen to God’s promises. God says Yes in Christ; we say Amen through Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every promise we want to claim is ours. It means every promise God made to his people is secured in Christ.

In a sentence. As surely as God is faithful, our message to you has not been yes and no at once. For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom Silas, Timothy and Paul preached among you, was not yes and no; in him it has always been yes. However many promises God has made, they are yes in Christ. And so through him we say Amen, to the glory of God.

For worship. Pick a promise of God in Scripture. In Christ, it is Yes for you. Say Amen to it today.
verseByVerse.note: Silvanus is Silas, who worked with Paul at Corinth. “Amen” means “it is true, so be it.”

verseByVerse.quote: And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us, and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.

And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ. Key words. “Establishes” (bebaioō, makes firm, confirms; a legal and commercial term for guaranteeing). God keeps believers firm in their union with Christ. Paul and the Corinthians are established together.

And has anointed us. Key words. “Anointed” (chriō, from which Christ, the Anointed One). As Christ was anointed with the Spirit, so are those in him (1 John 2:20, 27).

And who has also put his seal on us. Key words. A seal marked ownership and authenticity, and protected contents (Ephesians 1:13; 4:30). God has marked believers as his own.

And given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee. Key words. The word for “guarantee” (arrabōn) was used in business for a first payment or down payment, a pledge that the full amount would follow. The Spirit now is a foretaste and pledge of our full inheritance (5:5; Ephesians 1:14). In modern Greek the word means an engagement ring.

Where Christians differ: assurance of salvation. Some teach that believers cannot be sure of their final salvation in this life. Verdict: God himself establishes, anoints, seals and gives the Spirit as a guarantee. These are God’s acts, not ours, and they make the outcome certain. Believers can have a well-founded assurance, resting on God’s promises, the inner witness of the Spirit (Romans 8:16), and the evidence of his work in their lives (Westminster 18.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean every believer always feels assured. Assurance can be weakened by sin or trial. But God’s seal does not break.

In a sentence. Now it is God who makes both us and you stand firm in Christ. He anointed us, set his seal of ownership on us, and put his Spirit in our hearts as a deposit, guaranteeing what is to come.

On a Tuesday. You carry God’s seal and his down payment. Live today as one who belongs to him and is sure of the future.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership. The word for “guarantee” was used in business for a first instalment or deposit, pledging that the full payment will follow.

verseByVerse.quote: But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

But I call God to witness against me. Key words. A solemn oath: Paul stakes his life on what he says next.

It was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth. Key words. The real reason for the change of plans: if he had come, he would have had to come with discipline (1 Corinthians 4:21). He stayed away to give them time to repent, and wrote instead (2:1–4).

Not that we lord it over your faith. Key words. “Lord it over” (kyrieuō, dominate, rule as master). Apostolic authority is real, but it is not domination. No minister controls the faith of believers; faith answers to God (1 Peter 5:3).

But we work with you for your joy. Key words. “Work with” (synergoi, fellow workers). Ministers are helpers of believers’ joy.

For you stand firm in your faith. Key words. Their faith rests on God, not on Paul.

Where Christians differ: church authority over conscience. Some churches claim authority to bind believers’ consciences in matters beyond Scripture. Verdict: Church leaders have real authority to teach Scripture and to discipline, but no authority to rule over faith or bind the conscience beyond what God’s word requires. God alone is Lord of the conscience (Westminster 20.2). Leaders serve believers’ joy.

What it does not mean. It does not mean church leaders have no authority. Paul used his authority. It means authority serves, not dominates.

In a sentence. Paul calls God as his witness, and stakes his life on it: it was to spare you that he did not return to Corinth. Not that we rule over your faith; we work alongside you for your joy, because it is by faith you stand firm.

For worship. Pray for your pastors to lead not by domination but as helpers of your joy. And pray for your own faith to stand firm in God.

1.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the church of God that is at Corinth, with all the saints who are in the whole of Achaia:<sup>2</sup>Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.<sup>3</sup>Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort,<sup>4</sup>who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.<sup>5</sup>For as we share abundantly in Christ’s sufferings, so through Christ we share abundantly in comfort too.<sup>6</sup>If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; and if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which you experience when you patiently endure the same sufferings that we suffer.<sup>7</sup>Our hope for you is unshaken, for we know that as you share in our sufferings, you will also share in our comfort.<sup>8</sup>For we do not want you to be unaware, brothers, of the affliction we experienced in Asia. For we were so utterly burdened beyond our strength that we despaired of life itself.<sup>9</sup>Indeed, we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.<sup>10</sup>He delivered us from such a deadly peril, and he will deliver us. On him we have set our hope that he will deliver us again.<sup>11</sup>You also must help us by prayer, so that many will give thanks on our behalf for the blessing granted us through the prayers of many.<sup>12</sup>For our boast is this, the testimony of our conscience, that we behaved in the world with simplicity and godly sincerity, not by earthly wisdom but by the grace of God, and supremely so toward you.<sup>13</sup>For we are not writing to you anything other than what you read and understand and I hope you will fully understand—<sup>14</sup>just as you did partially understand us—that on the day of our Lord Jesus you will boast of us as we will boast of you.<sup>15</sup>Because I was sure of this, I wanted to come to you first, so that you might have a second experience of grace.<sup>16</sup>I wanted to visit you on my way to Macedonia, and to come back to you from Macedonia and have you send me on my way to Judea.<sup>17</sup>Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” at the same time?<sup>18</sup>As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No.<sup>19</sup>For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom we proclaimed among you, Silvanus and Timothy and I, was not Yes and No, but in him it is always Yes.<sup>20</sup>For all the promises of God find their Yes in him. That is why it is through him that we utter our Amen to God for his glory.<sup>21</sup>And it is God who establishes us with you in Christ, and has anointed us,<sup>22</sup>and who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee.<sup>23</sup>But I call God to witness against me—it was to spare you that I refrained from coming again to Corinth.<sup>24</sup>Not that we lord it over your faith, but we work with you for your joy, for you stand firm in your faith.

2.title: Forgiveness, the Aroma of Christ, and the Triumph of God
2.overview:
Paul continues to explain why he did not come back to Corinth. After the “painful visit”, in which one man publicly wronged him, he chose to write a tearful letter instead of returning to discipline them in person. The letter worked: the church disciplined the man. Now Paul’s concern is the opposite danger. The punishment has been enough. They must forgive him, comfort him and reaffirm their love, or Satan will take advantage, whether by crushing the man with excessive grief or by splitting the church.

Then Paul tells of his anxiety at Troas, where he could not wait for Titus’s news and left an open door to go to Macedonia. Before finishing the story (it resumes at 7:5), he bursts into thanks. God leads his servants in a Roman triumphal procession, captives of Christ on display, and through them spreads the fragrance of Christ everywhere: to some a smell of death, to others of life. Who is adequate for that? Not those who peddle God’s word for profit, but those who speak sincerely, as sent by God, in his sight.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Severe Letter and Forgiveness of the Offender
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why he wrote a severe letter instead of making another painful visit: he did not want to grieve the very people who give him joy, and he wrote in anguish and tears, out of love. The man who caused the trouble has wronged the whole church, not just Paul, and the church has now disciplined him. That is enough. Paul urges them to forgive, comfort and openly welcome him back, so that he is not crushed by sorrow, and so that Satan does not exploit the situation. Their response will show whether they obey in everything, including restoration.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage teaches that church discipline has a defined goal: restoration, not condemnation. This is the consistent NT pattern: Matthew 18:15–20, Galatians 6:1, 1 Corinthians 5. Discipline protects the community and pursues the restoration of the erring member. When the discipline has achieved its purpose, continuing to withhold forgiveness becomes its own sin — a sin that Satan is actively happy to see, because it fractures the community and communicates to the world that the church’s gospel of forgiveness does not apply internally.
verseByVerse.examples: A church elder who was removed from office after a moral failure has spent two years in genuine repentance and restoration. The leadership has quietly re-engaged him in limited service; but a vocal minority insists that any restoration is a betrayal of those he hurt. This passage does not minimise the hurt — Paul explicitly says the offender has caused grief to some extent (v. 5). But it insists that the goal of discipline is always restoration, and that the refusal to forgive when repentance is genuine is not faithfulness; it is a gift to the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained?

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 2 continues Paul’s explanation of his change of plans and then opens the great theme of the letter: the nature of gospel ministry. First, he explains that he did not come because he did not want another painful visit; instead he wrote a tearful letter out of love (vv. 1–4). Second, he addresses the man who had caused the trouble. The church has disciplined him and he has repented; now they must forgive, comfort and reaffirm their love for him, so that Satan does not gain an advantage through excessive severity (vv. 5–11). Third, Paul recalls his anxiety waiting for Titus, and then bursts into thanks: God leads his servants in Christ’s triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of Christ through them, a fragrance of life to some and death to others. No one is sufficient for that, but Paul speaks sincerely, as one sent by God, not as a peddler of God’s word (vv. 12–17).

For I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you. Key words. This painful visit is not recorded in Acts; it came between 1 and 2 Corinthians. “Painful” (lypē, grief, sorrow). Paul had come, been publicly opposed, and left grieved.

For if I cause you pain, who is there to make me glad but the one whom I have pained? Key words. Paul’s joy is bound up with them. If he grieves them, who will cheer him? Love makes the pastor’s happiness depend on his people’s well-being.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul avoided confrontation. He confronted in writing. It means he chose the way that would cause least harm.

In a sentence. So Paul decided not to make another painful visit to you. For if he grieves you, who is left to make him glad except the very people he has grieved?

On a Tuesday. When you must confront someone, ask God for wisdom about the best way and time.
verseByVerse.note: This painful visit is not recorded in Acts; it came between 1 and 2 Corinthians.

verseByVerse.quote: And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I wrote as I did, so that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice, for I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears, not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you.

And I wrote as I did. Key words. This severe letter is probably lost; some think it is part of chapters 10–13. Most scholars think it was a separate letter, since 1 Corinthians does not fit the description of a letter written with many tears.

So that when I came I might not suffer pain from those who should have made me rejoice. Key words. He wrote first, so that when he came, things would be resolved.

For I felt sure of all of you, that my joy would be the joy of you all. Key words. He trusted that they wanted what he wanted.

For I wrote to you out of much affliction and anguish of heart and with many tears. Key words. “Anguish” (synochē, distress, being squeezed). The letter cost him greatly. Faithful rebuke is painful for the one who gives it too.

Not to cause you pain but to let you know the abundant love that I have for you. Key words. The purpose of rebuke is love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend (Proverbs 27:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean rebuke should be avoided because it hurts. It means rebuke should flow from love and tears.

In a sentence. Paul wrote as he did so that when he came he would not be grieved by those who should make him glad. He was confident that you would all share his joy. He wrote out of great distress and anguish of heart, with many tears, not to grieve you but to show you how much he loves you.

For worship. If you must correct someone, pray first, and let them see your love.
verseByVerse.note: This severe letter is probably lost; some think it is part of 2 Corinthians 10–13.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if anyone has caused pain, he has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you.

Now if anyone has caused pain. Key words. The offender is unnamed; he is most likely not the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5, but someone who publicly opposed or insulted Paul during the painful visit. Paul tactfully avoids naming him.

He has caused it not to me, but in some measure—not to put it too severely—to all of you. Key words. Paul refuses to make it personal. The offence was against the whole church. “Not to put it too severely”: Paul is careful not to overstate.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was not hurt. It means he will not make his hurt the issue.

In a sentence. If anyone has caused grief, he has not so much grieved Paul as he has grieved all of you to some extent, not to put it too strongly.

On a Tuesday. When someone wrongs you, resist making it all about you. Think of the wider good.
verseByVerse.note: The offender is unnamed; he is most likely not the man disciplined in 1 Corinthians 5 but someone who had publicly opposed Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough, so you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.

For such a one, this punishment by the majority is enough. Key words. “Punishment” (epitimia, rebuke, penalty): church discipline. By the majority: the church acted together, though perhaps a minority wanted more severity or none. It has done its work.

So you should rather turn to forgive and comfort him. Key words. “Forgive” (charizomai, show grace). “Comfort” (parakaleō, encourage). Discipline aims at restoration. Once there is repentance, the church must restore warmly (Galatians 6:1).

Or he may be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Key words. “Overwhelmed” (katapinō, swallowed up). Too much severity can crush a repentant sinner into despair.

What it does not mean. It does not mean discipline should be skipped. It means discipline must end in forgiveness when there is repentance.

In a sentence. The punishment the majority gave him is enough. Now you should forgive and comfort him instead, so that he is not overwhelmed by too much grief.

For worship. Is there someone who has repented whom you have not fully forgiven? Forgive and comfort them, as Christ has you.

verseByVerse.quote: So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him.

So I beg you to reaffirm your love for him. Key words. “Reaffirm” (kyroō, ratify, confirm officially): a legal term. The church should formally and publicly restore him, as publicly as it disciplined him. Not just tolerate, but love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean pretending nothing happened. It means welcoming him back fully.

In a sentence. So Paul urges you to confirm your love for him publicly.

On a Tuesday. When someone repents, do not keep them at arm’s length. Show them your love clearly.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is why I wrote, that I might test you and know whether you are obedient in everything.

For this is why I wrote, that I might test you. Key words. “Test” (dokimē, proof, character proven by testing). The severe letter tested whether they would respond to apostolic authority.

And know whether you are obedient in everything. Key words. They passed the test by disciplining the offender. Now obedience means forgiving him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wanted blind obedience to himself. He wanted obedience to Christ, expressed through apostolic teaching.

In a sentence. Another reason Paul wrote was to see whether you would stand the test and be obedient in everything.

For worship. Obedience includes the hard step of forgiveness. Ask God to make you obedient in everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ, so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.

Anyone whom you forgive, I also forgive. Key words. Paul joins the church in forgiveness.

Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ. Key words. Paul plays down his own hurt. His forgiveness is for the church’s good, done before Christ’s face.

So that we would not be outwitted by Satan. Key words. “Outwitted” (pleonekteō, take advantage of, defraud). Satan uses unforgiveness to divide churches, to crush repentant sinners, and to make discipline harsh. Harsh, unending discipline plays into his hands as much as no discipline at all.

For we are not ignorant of his designs. Key words. “Designs” (noēmata, schemes, plots). Christians should know Satan’s tactics (Ephesians 6:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Satan is behind every problem. It means he exploits our sins, including the sin of unforgiveness.

In a sentence. Anyone you forgive, Paul forgives too. And what he has forgiven, if there was anything to forgive, he has forgiven in the sight of Christ for your sake, so that Satan might not outwit us. For we know his schemes.

On a Tuesday. Unforgiveness gives Satan a foothold (Ephesians 4:26–27). Forgive today, and close the door on him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul resumes the story of his journey. At Troas there was an open door for the gospel, but he was too anxious about Corinth to stay when Titus did not arrive, so he went on to Macedonia. Before telling what happened next, he breaks into thanks. He pictures God leading him as a captive in Christ’s victory parade, with the scent of the knowledge of Christ spreading wherever he goes. To some that scent means death, to others life. No one is adequate for such a task, but Paul, unlike those who sell a diluted message, speaks sincerely as one sent by God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The triumphal procession image is rich and theologically precise. In a Roman triumph, captives were led in chains behind the victor — some to be executed at the procession’s end, some to be enslaved. Paul’s use of the image for himself is deliberately surprising: the apostle is not the victorious general but a captive in Christ’s train. Yet this is not degradation — to be a captive of Christ, led in his triumph, is the highest possible dignity. The early church’s constant refrain — “slave of Christ” (doulos Christou) — captures the same paradox: absolute belonging to Christ is absolute dignity.

The double effect of the gospel (life to some, death to others) is grounded in passages like Isaiah 8:14 (the stone of stumbling) and Luke 2:34 (this child is set for the falling and rising of many). The gospel is not universally received, but this is not a failure of the gospel; it is a revelation of the human heart. The same sun that softens wax hardens clay — not because the sun changed but because the materials are different.
verseByVerse.examples: A missionary returns from several years in a largely unresponsive field and struggles with a sense of failure — very few converts, considerable opposition. This passage speaks to him directly: the task is not to produce results but to be the aroma of Christ. The spreading of the fragrance is the mission; the effect — life or death — belongs to God and to the hearts of those who encounter it. Faithfulness is measured by the aroma, not by the response.

verseByVerse.quote: When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord, my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.

When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ. Key words. Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia, near ancient Troy. Paul went there after leaving Ephesus.

Even though a door was opened for me in the Lord. Key words. A great opportunity for the gospel.

My spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. Key words. Titus was a trusted co-worker who had carried the severe letter to Corinth. Paul was desperate to hear how they had responded. “Not at rest” (anesis, no relief).

So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia. Key words. Paul left an open door because of his anxiety for the Corinthians. Honest about his weakness. The story resumes in 7:5.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was wrong to leave. Love for the Corinthians was also gospel work.

In a sentence. When Paul went to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ and found that the Lord had opened a door for him, he still had no peace of mind, because he did not find his brother Titus there. So he said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.

For worship. Bring your anxieties for others to God. He cares about your restlessness.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast of Asia. Titus was a trusted Gentile co-worker, sent to Corinth with the severe letter.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.

But thanks be to God. Key words. A sudden burst of praise, as Paul remembers how God answered his anxiety (7:6).

Who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession. Key words. A Roman triumph was a victory parade through the city; captives marched in chains behind the conquering general, often to execution. “Leads in triumph” (thriambeuō). Paul pictures himself as one of Christ’s captives, conquered by him on the Damascus road, now displayed in his victory march. Not a picture of Paul’s triumph, but of Christ’s triumph over Paul, which looks like weakness and suffering (1 Corinthians 4:9).

And through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere. Key words. In a triumph, incense was burned along the route, filling the city with fragrance. Through Paul’s preaching, the knowledge of Christ spreads like a fragrance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Christian life is constant success. Paul speaks of triumph right after admitting his restless anxiety.

In a sentence. But thanks be to God, who always leads us as captives in Christ’s victory parade, and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of knowing him.

On a Tuesday. You are Christ’s captive, and part of his victory. Let your life spread the fragrance of Christ today.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman triumph was a victory parade through the city; captives were led in chains, and incense was burned along the route.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing, to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?

For we are the aroma of Christ to God. Key words. “Aroma” (euōdia, sweet smell), the word used of sacrifices pleasing to God (Genesis 8:21; Ephesians 5:2). The gospel ministry is first of all an offering to God, pleasing to him whatever the results.

Among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing. Key words. Two groups, as in 1 Corinthians 1:18. The same message is heard by both.

To one a fragrance from death to death. Key words. To those perishing, the gospel smells of death: a crucified man, and their own judgement. Rejecting it leads to final death.

To the other a fragrance from life to life. Key words. To those being saved, it is the scent of life, leading to eternal life. In the triumph, the incense meant death for the captives and life for the victors.

Who is sufficient for these things? Key words. “Sufficient” (hikanos, adequate, competent). Who is equal to such a weighty task, with eternal consequences? No one, in himself. Paul answers in 3:5: our sufficiency is from God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers cause people to perish. The gospel reveals and confirms what people are.

In a sentence. For we are to God the sweet smell of Christ among those being saved and those perishing. To the one we are the smell of death leading to death; to the other, the fragrance of life leading to life. And who is up to such a task?

For worship. Your faithful witness is pleasing to God, whatever the response. Offer it to him today.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.

For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word. Key words. A peddler (kapēleuō) was a street trader known for watering down his wine or cheating customers. Some preachers were selling the gospel for profit, diluting it to please their audience. “So many”: a pointed reference to the rival teachers in Corinth.

But as men of sincerity. Key words. “Sincerity” (eilikrineia, purity, unmixed).

As commissioned by God. Key words. Literally, as from God. Paul’s message comes from God, not his own ideas.

In the sight of God we speak in Christ. Key words. Before God’s eyes, united to Christ. Ministers answer to God for every word.

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should never be paid. It means they must never preach for money, or change the message to please people.

In a sentence. Unlike so many, we do not peddle God’s word for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as people sent from God.

On a Tuesday. When you speak of Christ, speak sincerely, as before God. Do not water down the message to please others.
verseByVerse.note: A peddler was a street trader known for watering down his wine to increase profits.
