Indeed, what I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, has been for your sake in the presence of Christ,<sup>11</sup>so that we would not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs.<sup>12</sup>When I came to Troas to preach the gospel of Christ, even though a door was opened for me in the Lord,<sup>13</sup>my spirit was not at rest because I did not find my brother Titus there. So I took leave of them and went on to Macedonia.<sup>14</sup>But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere.<sup>15</sup>For we are the aroma of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing,<sup>16</sup>to one a fragrance from death to death, to the other a fragrance from life to life. Who is sufficient for these things?<sup>17</sup>For we are not, like so many, peddlers of God’s word, but as men of sincerity, as commissioned by God, in the sight of God we speak in Christ.

3.title: Letters of Recommendation, the New Covenant, and the Unveiled Face
3.overview:
The visiting teachers in Corinth carried letters of recommendation and probably claimed the authority of Moses. Paul answers both claims. He needs no letter: the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts, just as God promised through Jeremiah and Ezekiel that the new covenant would write his law on hearts, not stone. His adequacy comes from God, who has made him a minister of that new covenant, “not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Then Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Exodus 34. When Moses came down from Sinai with the law, his face shone so that Israel could not look at him, and he put on a veil. Paul argues: if the ministry that brought condemnation came with such glory, a glory that was being set aside, how much greater is the ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness, which lasts. To this day a veil lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without Christ; but whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. And all believers, with unveiled faces, behold the glory of the Lord and are being transformed into his image, from one degree of glory to another, by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Ministers of the New Covenant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s rivals came with letters of recommendation. Paul needs none: the Corinthian church is his letter, written by the Spirit on human hearts rather than in ink or on stone, just as the prophets promised for the new covenant. His confidence rests not on his own ability but on God, who has made him a servant of that new covenant. The old covenant, written on stone, could only condemn; the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.theology: The contrast between letter and Spirit (v. 6) — “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” — is one of the most misunderstood phrases in Paul. It does not mean that the written word of Scripture is deadly and only spiritual illumination gives life (a Gnostic-leaning interpretation). In context, “the letter” refers specifically to the Mosaic law written on stone — the external commandment that makes demands it cannot empower fulfilling, that reveals sin it cannot remove. The Spirit gives life by doing what the letter could not: writing the law on the heart, enabling obedience from the inside. This is the Jeremiah 31/Ezekiel 36 promise in Paul’s theological shorthand.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation that prides itself on doctrinal correctness — its members can pass any biblical literacy test, articulate the five points of Calvinism, and explain every Confession — but whose relational life is cold and whose evangelistic impact is minimal. The letter/Spirit contrast is not a critique of doctrine or written Scripture; it is a diagnosis of the difference between external knowledge of the truth and inward transformation by it. The new covenant minister’s goal is not to fill heads but to be the instrument through whom the Spirit writes on hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you?

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 3 is one of the Bible’s great chapters on the difference between the old covenant and the new. The rival teachers in Corinth arrived with letters of recommendation and perhaps stressed the law of Moses. Paul says the Corinthians themselves are his letter, written by the Spirit on their hearts, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel had promised for the new covenant (vv. 1–3). His sufficiency comes from God, who made him a minister of a new covenant, not of the letter that kills, but of the Spirit who gives life (vv. 4–6). Then he compares the two ministries. The old covenant, carved on stone, came with real glory, shining on Moses’ face. But it was a ministry of condemnation and death, and its glory was fading. The new covenant ministry of the Spirit and of righteousness has a far greater, permanent glory (vv. 7–11). Moses veiled his face; a veil still lies over the hearts of those who read the old covenant without Christ. When anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is removed. And all believers, with unveiled faces, behold the Lord’s glory and are being transformed into his image, from glory to glory, by the Spirit (vv. 12–18).

Are we beginning to commend ourselves again? Key words. Paul’s defence in chapters 1–2 might look like self-promotion. He anticipates the charge.

Or do we need, as some do, letters of recommendation to you, or from you? Key words. Letters of recommendation were common for travellers; Paul’s rivals had brought them, perhaps from Jerusalem, and wanted new ones from Corinth. Paul had written such letters for others (Romans 16:1; 1 Corinthians 16:3). But he does not need one to the church he founded.

What it does not mean. It does not mean letters of recommendation are wrong. It means Paul’s ministry needs no paper credentials among people he brought to Christ.

In a sentence. Are we starting to recommend ourselves again? Or do we need, like some people, letters of introduction to you or from you?

On a Tuesday. The best recommendation of your faith is not words about yourself but changed lives around you.
verseByVerse.note: Letters of recommendation were common for travellers; Paul’s rivals at Corinth came with them.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves are our letter of recommendation, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all. And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.

You yourselves are our letter of recommendation. Key words. The Corinthian church is Paul’s credential (1 Corinthians 9:2).

Written on our hearts. Key words. Paul carries them in his heart with love. Some manuscripts read your hearts.

To be known and read by all. Key words. Everyone can see what God has done in Corinth.

And you show that you are a letter from Christ delivered by us. Key words. Christ is the author; Paul the delivery man, or the secretary.

Written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God. Key words. The Spirit wrote on their lives.

Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts. Key words. The Ten Commandments were carved on stone tablets (Exodus 24:12; 31:18). But God promised a new covenant in which he would write his law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33), and give hearts of flesh instead of stone, by his Spirit (Ezekiel 11:19; 36:26–27). That promise is fulfilled in the Corinthians.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law on stone was bad. It was God’s law. But written on stone, it could not change hearts. The Spirit writes it within.

In a sentence. You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, known and read by everyone. You show that you are a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone tablets but on human hearts.

For worship. If you are in Christ, the Spirit has written God’s law on your heart. Thank him for the new heart he has given you.

parallels.desc: tablets of stone, written with the finger of God
a heart of flesh

verseByVerse.quote: Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God,

Such is the confidence that we have through Christ toward God. Key words. Paul’s confidence rests on what God has done, through Christ, and stands before God’s scrutiny.

Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us. Key words. The answer to 2:16, who is sufficient? “Sufficient” (hikanos). Not Paul, in himself.

But our sufficiency is from God. Key words. God supplies everything needed for ministry. Interestingly, one Old Testament name of God in the Greek translation is Hikanos, the Sufficient One (Ruth 1:20–21, translating Shaddai).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers need no training or effort. It means their ability to change hearts comes from God alone.

In a sentence. Such confidence we have through Christ before God. Not that we are competent in ourselves to claim anything as our own; our competence comes from God.

On a Tuesday. You may feel inadequate for what God has called you to. Good. Your sufficiency is from God. Ask him.

verseByVerse.quote: who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

Who has made us sufficient to be ministers of a new covenant. Key words. The new covenant, promised in Jeremiah 31:31–34 and inaugurated by Christ’s blood (1 Corinthians 11:25). Paul serves it.

Not of the letter but of the Spirit. Key words. The “letter” is the law written on stone, which could condemn but not give life. The Spirit is the life-giver who writes God’s law on hearts.

For the letter kills. Key words. The law, holy and good as it is, condemns sinners (Romans 7:10–11; Galatians 3:10). It shows what is required and pronounces death on those who fail, but gives no power to obey.

But the Spirit gives life. Key words. The Spirit regenerates, gives new life, and enables obedience (John 6:63; Romans 8:2, 11).

Where Christians differ: the letter and the spirit. Since Origen, some have read this verse as a principle of interpretation: the literal meaning of Scripture kills, but the spiritual or allegorical meaning gives life. Verdict: Paul is not speaking about methods of reading Scripture, but about two covenants: the law written on stone, which condemns, and the Spirit’s new covenant work, which gives life. The Reformers rightly insisted on the plain, literal-grammatical meaning of Scripture, read in the light of Christ. The law is not abolished as God’s moral standard for believers; but it cannot justify or give life. Only the Spirit, through the gospel, does that.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the law is evil (Romans 7:12). It means the law alone cannot save.

In a sentence. He has made us competent as ministers of a new covenant, not of the written code but of the Spirit; for the written code brings death, but the Spirit gives life.

For worship. Thank God for the Spirit who gives you life, where the law alone could only condemn you.
verseByVerse.note: The “letter” is the law written on stone, which could condemn but not give life.

parallels.desc: a new covenant

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–18 — The Fading Glory and the Surpassing Glory; the Unveiled Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul compares the two covenants through the story of Moses’ shining face. The law came with real glory, so bright that Israel could not look at Moses. But that ministry brought condemnation and was temporary. The ministry of the Spirit, which brings righteousness and lasts, has a far greater glory. Moses veiled his face; Paul speaks openly. A veil still lies over the hearts of those who read Moses without Christ, but it is removed whenever anyone turns to the Lord. The Lord meets us now by the Spirit, who brings freedom, and all believers, seeing his glory with unveiled faces, are being gradually changed into his likeness.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Moses passage (Ex. 34) in Paul’s reading makes a claim that has been debated since the patristic period: Paul appears to say that Moses wore the veil to prevent the Israelites from seeing the glory’s end (v. 13), whereas Exodus dwells on the Israelites’ fear of his shining face. Paul is reading the text through the lens of its fulfilment in Christ: the entire Mosaic economy was a temporary arrangement pointing beyond itself, and the veil that covered Moses’s face symbolises the veil that covers the hearts of those who read him without recognising his Christological pointing.

The transformation passage (v. 18) is the key text for the Reformed understanding of sanctification as a work of the Spirit through the Word. Beholding — katoptrizomenoi (gazing as in a mirror, or reflecting as a mirror) — is the mechanism. The Word presents Christ; the Spirit uses the Word to produce in the believer the image they behold. John Owen, commenting on this verse, says that the primary means of sanctification is not moral effort but contemplation of the glory of Christ as revealed in the gospel.
verseByVerse.examples: A spiritual director works with a young Christian who is exhausted by the effort of sanctification — constantly striving, measuring, failing, striving again. She introduces him to the practice of deliberate meditation on specific passages that describe the character and glory of Christ, asking him to rest in the image rather than immediately applying it. After several months he reports something shifting in his desires and responses — not through effort but through what this verse would call beholding. The transformation is from the Lord who is the Spirit; the means is the unveiled face gazing at glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory, which was being brought to an end, will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory?

Now if the ministry of death, carved in letters on stone. Key words. The old covenant, centred on the law given at Sinai. It is called a ministry of death because, for sinners, its result was condemnation.

Came with such glory that the Israelites could not gaze at Moses’ face because of its glory. Key words. When Moses came down from Sinai, his face shone so brightly that the people were afraid (Exodus 34:29–35). The old covenant really was glorious; it came from God.

Which was being brought to an end. Key words. “Brought to an end” (katargeō, fading, being set aside). The glory on Moses’ face faded, a picture of the temporary nature of the old covenant (Hebrews 8:13).

Will not the ministry of the Spirit have even more glory? Key words. An argument from lesser to greater. If the old was glorious, how much more the new.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament has no value. It means its covenant arrangements were preparatory, pointing to Christ.

In a sentence. Now if the ministry that brought death, engraved in letters on stone, came with such glory that the Israelites could not look steadily at Moses’ face because of its glory, fading though it was, will not the ministry of the Spirit be even more glorious?

On a Tuesday. You live under a more glorious covenant than Moses did. Do not settle for less than the Spirit’s life.

parallels.desc: the skin of Moses’ face shone

verseByVerse.quote: For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, the ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory.

For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation. Key words. The law condemned sinners.

The ministry of righteousness must far exceed it in glory. Key words. The new covenant brings righteousness: justification, God’s gift of a right standing through Christ (5:21; Romans 3:21–22). Giving righteousness is far more glorious than pronouncing condemnation.

Indeed, in this case, what once had glory has come to have no glory at all, because of the glory that surpasses it. Key words. Like a candle in sunlight, or the moon at noon. The old covenant’s glory is real, but outshone.

For if what was being brought to an end came with glory, much more will what is permanent have glory. Key words. The old was temporary; the new is permanent (menō, remaining). The new covenant will never be replaced.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the moral law has ended. The covenant administration ended; God’s moral will is now written on hearts.

In a sentence. If the ministry that brought condemnation was glorious, how much more glorious is the ministry that brings righteousness! What was glorious has no glory now compared with the surpassing glory. And if what was fading away came with glory, how much greater is the glory of what lasts!

For worship. Praise God for the ministry of righteousness that declared you right with him. It is more glorious than Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have such a hope, we are very bold, not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face so that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end.

Since we have such a hope, we are very bold. Key words. “Bold” (parrēsia, openness, frankness, freedom of speech). Paul speaks openly, without hiding anything.

Not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face. Key words. Moses wore a veil after speaking to the people (Exodus 34:33–35).

So that the Israelites might not gaze at the outcome of what was being brought to an end. Key words. “Outcome” (telos, end). Paul interprets the veil: it kept Israel from seeing the glory fade, a sign that the old covenant was temporary. It also symbolised that Israel could not see the full meaning of the old covenant, which pointed to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Moses was deceitful. Paul is drawing out the symbolic meaning of the veil.

In a sentence. Since we have such a hope, we are very open, unlike Moses, who put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from seeing the end of what was passing away.

On a Tuesday. Be open and bold about the gospel. You have nothing to hide.

parallels.desc: he put a veil over his face

verseByVerse.quote: But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted, because only through Christ is it taken away. Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts.

But their minds were hardened. Key words. “Hardened” (pōroō, made callous, Romans 11:7). Israel’s unbelief was not just lack of information but hardness of heart.

For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains unlifted. Key words. The old covenant: the Old Testament Scriptures, especially the law. The first use of this phrase for the Old Testament. In the synagogue, the Scriptures were read, but not understood in their true meaning, which is Christ (Luke 24:27; John 5:39).

Because only through Christ is it taken away. Key words. Christ is the key to the Old Testament. Without him, it remains veiled.

Yes, to this day whenever Moses is read a veil lies over their hearts. Key words. “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue (Acts 15:21). The veil has moved from Moses’ face to the readers’ hearts.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish people are worse than others. Every unbeliever has a veil over the heart (4:3–4). And it does not mean the Old Testament is obscure in itself. It is clear to those who see Christ in it.

In a sentence. But their minds were made dull, and to this day the same veil remains when the old covenant is read. It has not been removed, because only in Christ is it taken away. Even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil covers their hearts.

For worship. Pray for Jewish friends and all who read the Scriptures without seeing Christ. Ask God to lift the veil.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses” here means the books of Moses, read aloud each Sabbath in the synagogue.

verseByVerse.quote: But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.

But when one turns to the Lord. Key words. “Turns” (epistrephō, converts, returns): repentance and faith. Paul echoes Exodus: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he removed the veil (Exodus 34:34). Whoever turns to the Lord, as Moses did, has the veil taken away.

The veil is removed. Key words. “Removed” (periaireō, taken away completely). Passive: God removes it. Then the Scriptures become clear, and the glory of Christ is seen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we remove the veil ourselves. Turning to the Lord is itself God’s gift (4:6).

In a sentence. But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.

On a Tuesday. If Scripture seems veiled to you, turn to the Lord and ask him to open your eyes as you read.
verseByVerse.note: Paul echoes Exodus: whenever Moses went in before the LORD, he removed the veil.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

Now the Lord is the Spirit. Key words. The Lord in verse 16, in Exodus, is Yahweh. Paul explains: in the new covenant, turning to the Lord means encountering the Spirit, who applies Christ’s work and removes the veil. The Spirit is the Lord, fully divine, and he is the Spirit of the Lord, distinct and yet one with him.

And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom. Key words. Freedom (eleutheria): from the veil, from the condemnation of the law, from bondage to sin and death (Romans 8:2; Galatians 5:1), and freedom of access to God’s presence.

Where Christians differ: is the Lord the Spirit? Some (modalists) take this verse to mean the Son and the Spirit are the same person. Verdict: Paul distinguishes the Spirit and the Lord in the same verse: the Spirit of the Lord. He is saying that the Lord of the Exodus passage is now encountered through the Spirit, who is himself the Lord, fully God. The Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct persons, one God (2 Corinthians 13:14).

What it does not mean. It does not mean freedom to sin. Spirit-given freedom is freedom to obey and serve (Galatians 5:13).

In a sentence. Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

For worship. Thank the Spirit for the freedom he has given you: from condemnation, from sin’s power, and into God’s presence.

verseByVerse.quote: And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.

And we all, with unveiled face. Key words. All believers, not just Moses or apostles. In the old covenant, only Moses saw God’s glory, and veiled it. In the new, every believer’s face is unveiled.

Beholding the glory of the Lord. Key words. “Beholding” (katoptrizomai, looking at as in a mirror, or reflecting as a mirror). We see the Lord’s glory in the face of Christ (4:6), as revealed in the gospel and Scripture.

Are being transformed into the same image. Key words. “Transformed” (metamorphoō, as in Romans 12:2). Present and passive: we are continually being changed by God. Into the same image: the image of Christ (Romans 8:29). We become like what we behold.

From one degree of glory to another. Key words. Literally, from glory to glory. A gradual, progressive change. Moses’ glory faded; ours increases. This is sanctification, ending in glorification.

For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit. Key words. The Spirit does the transforming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean transformation is instant or that we become perfect in this life. It means steady growth as we look at Christ.

In a sentence. And all of us, with faces unveiled, see the Lord’s glory as in a mirror, and are being changed into his likeness with ever-increasing glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. You become like what you look at. Spend time today looking at Christ in his word.

4.title: Treasure in Jars of Clay
4.overview:
Paul has described the surpassing glory of the new covenant ministry. Now he faces the obvious objection: if the ministry is so glorious, why is the minister so unimpressive, so beaten up, so weak? The Corinthians, living in a city that admired polish, power and success, were embarrassed by an apostle who looked like a failure.

Paul answers in three movements. First, he does not lose heart or use tricks; he openly states the truth. If some cannot see it, it is because Satan, “the god of this world”, has blinded them, while the God who said “Let light shine out of darkness” has shone into believers’ hearts with the light of his glory in the face of Christ. Second, this treasure is kept in clay jars, cheap and fragile, so that everyone can see the power is God’s. Paul is afflicted but not crushed, perplexed but not in despair, struck down but not destroyed; he carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may appear. Third, he does not lose heart, because although his outer self is wasting away, his inner self is renewed daily, and this light, momentary affliction is producing an eternal weight of glory. So he looks not at what is seen, which is temporary, but at what is unseen, which is eternal.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Light Shining in Darkness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Because his ministry is a gift of mercy, Paul does not give up, and he refuses tricks or distortion of God’s word, relying on open truth. If some cannot see the gospel, it is because Satan has blinded them. Paul preaches Christ as Lord, not himself, and regards himself as their servant. Conversion is God’s work, like creation: the God who first commanded light has shone into believers’ hearts so that they see his glory in the face of Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The identification of Christ as “the image of God” (v. 4) is one of Paul’s most direct Christological statements, paralleled in Colossians 1:15. Christ is not merely like God or a representative of God; he is the very image — the precise visible representation — of the invisible God. To see Christ is to see God (John 14:9). The glory of God is concentrated in the face of Jesus Christ (v. 6) — not in theophanies or visions or mystical experiences, but in the specific person of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen.

The parallel between Gen. 1:3 (“Let there be light”) and v. 6 (“God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone in our hearts”) is one of the NT’s most striking statements about the nature of conversion: it is a creative act of God, analogous to the original creation. Regeneration is not human spiritual development; it is the same divine fiat that created light from nothing. This is the Reformers’ point: regeneration precedes and enables faith; it is not faith that produces the new birth but the new birth that produces faith.
verseByVerse.examples: A campus minister explains the gospel to a sharp philosophy student who has engaged with every argument and remains unconvinced. He is tempted to find a better argument. This passage suggests a different diagnosis: the issue may not be intellectual but spiritual — a blinding that no amount of superior argument can overcome. The appropriate response includes not abandoning the argument (Paul commends himself to the conscience) but adding sustained prayer for the God who speaks light into darkness to do so in this particular darkness.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God, we do not lose heart. But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word, but by the open statement of the truth we would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 4 shows how glorious new-covenant ministry actually looks in practice: like a treasure in a clay jar. First, Paul preaches openly, without trickery or tampering with God’s word. If people do not see, it is because Satan, the god of this age, has blinded them; but God, who said let light shine out of darkness, shines into hearts to show the glory of God in the face of Christ (vv. 1–6). Second, this treasure is carried in weak, breakable human vessels, so that the power is clearly God’s. Paul is pressed, perplexed, persecuted and struck down, but never crushed, despairing, forsaken or destroyed; he carries Jesus’ death in his body so that Jesus’ life may be seen (vv. 7–12). Third, he keeps speaking because he believes in the resurrection (vv. 13–15). So he does not lose heart: the outer self is wasting away, but the inner self is renewed daily, and present troubles are light and brief compared with the eternal weight of glory they are preparing (vv. 16–18).

Therefore, having this ministry by the mercy of God. Key words. This ministry: the new covenant ministry of chapter 3. By mercy: Paul, the former persecutor, received it as pure mercy (1 Timothy 1:12–16).

We do not lose heart. Key words. “Lose heart” (enkakeō, give up, become discouraged). Repeated in verse 16. Despite opposition and suffering, Paul does not quit.

But we have renounced disgraceful, underhanded ways. Key words. Literally, the hidden things of shame. Secret methods one would be ashamed of. Perhaps the rival teachers accused Paul of hidden motives.

We refuse to practice cunning or to tamper with God’s word. Key words. “Cunning” (panourgia, craftiness, trickery). “Tamper” (doloō, adulterate, falsify, as of watering down wine; compare 2:17). Paul does not twist Scripture or manipulate people.

But by the open statement of the truth. Key words. “Open statement” (phanerōsis, manifestation). He sets out the truth plainly.

We would commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God. Key words. He appeals to conscience, not emotion or cleverness. And he does it before God, who sees all.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persuasion is wrong. Paul persuaded (5:11). It means persuasion must be honest.

In a sentence. So since through God’s mercy we have this ministry, we do not give up. We have rejected secret and shameful ways; we do not use deception or distort God’s word. Instead, by setting out the truth plainly, we commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.

On a Tuesday. When you share the gospel, be honest and plain. No tricks, no pressure, no hidden agendas.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, to keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

And even if our gospel is veiled. Key words. Some said Paul’s gospel was obscure. Paul answers: the problem is not the gospel but the hearers.

It is veiled to those who are perishing. Key words. Those on the way to destruction (2:15).

In their case the god of this world. Key words. “The god of this world” is Satan, the ruler of this age (John 12:31; 14:30; Ephesians 2:2; 1 John 5:19). “This world” is literally this age.

Has blinded the minds of the unbelievers. Key words. Satan blinds unbelievers’ minds so that they cannot see the truth. Unbelief is not just intellectual; it is spiritual blindness.

To keep them from seeing the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ. Key words. The gospel shines with Christ’s glory. Satan’s aim is to keep people from seeing it.

Who is the image of God. Key words. “Image” (eikōn). Christ perfectly reveals God (Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3; John 14:9). To see Christ is to see God.

Where Christians differ: the god of this world. Some ancient heretics (Marcion and the Gnostics) took this to mean the God of the Old Testament, a lesser, evil god. Verdict: The god of this age is Satan, who is called god because unbelievers serve him and he holds sway over the present evil age. His power is real but limited and temporary, under God’s sovereign control (Job 1:12), and already defeated at the cross (Colossians 2:15). There is one true God, who made the world and rules it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean unbelievers have no responsibility. They love darkness rather than light (John 3:19). Satan blinds those who refuse the truth.

In a sentence. And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing. The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so that they cannot see the light of the gospel that displays the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

For worship. Pray for unbelievers you know. Ask God to defeat the blinding power of Satan and open their eyes.
verseByVerse.note: “The god of this world” is Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.

For what we proclaim is not ourselves. Key words. Paul’s rivals were promoting themselves. Paul does not preach himself: his experiences, his gifts, his success.

But Jesus Christ as Lord. Key words. The content of the gospel: Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9; 1 Corinthians 12:3).

With ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. Key words. “Servants” (douloi, slaves). Christ is Lord; preachers are slaves of the church, for Jesus’ sake. The opposite of lording over (1:24).

What it does not mean. It does not mean preachers should never share personal experience. Paul does in this very letter. It means preachers must never make themselves the message.

In a sentence. For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.

On a Tuesday. When you talk about your faith, make Jesus the hero, not yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.

For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness.” Key words. An echo of creation: let there be light (Genesis 1:3), and of Isaiah 9:2: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. The same God who created light in the beginning creates light in the heart.

Has shone in our hearts. Key words. Conversion is a new creation (5:17). Paul is thinking of his own conversion, when a light from heaven shone around him (Acts 9:3). Every believer has had God shine into their heart.

To give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. Key words. The glory of God, which Moses could not see directly (Exodus 33:18–23), is now seen in the face of Jesus Christ. To know Christ is to know the glory of God.

Where Christians differ: how does conversion happen? Some believe that God offers light, and humans by their own will choose to open their eyes. Verdict: The picture is creation. As darkness did not cooperate with God in creating light, the blinded heart does not cooperate in its own illumination. God shines in; the result is sight and faith. This is regeneration, God’s sovereign, effectual work (Ephesians 2:4–5; Westminster 10.1–2). The person then believes freely and gladly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean conversion is always sudden or dramatic, as Paul’s was. The light may dawn gradually. But it is always God’s work.

In a sentence. For God, who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” made his light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of God’s glory displayed in the face of Christ.

For worship. If you see the glory of God in Jesus, God has shone into your heart. Praise him for your new creation.

parallels.desc: let there be light

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Treasure in Jars of Clay
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The treasure of the gospel is carried in fragile, ordinary containers, so that the power is clearly God’s. Paul describes his life as a series of near-defeats that never become defeats: pressed but not crushed, bewildered but not without hope, hunted but not abandoned, knocked down but not destroyed. He shares Jesus’ dying so that Jesus’ life can be seen in him, and his suffering brings life to others. Like the psalmist, he believes and therefore speaks, sure that the God who raised Jesus will raise him too. All of it serves the spread of grace and the increase of thanks to God.
verseByVerse.theology:
The four contrasts in vv. 8–9 are not merely biographical observations; they are a theological programme. The pattern of affliction-but-not-destroyed is the pattern of the cross applied to the messengers of the cross. The phrase rendered “the death of Jesus” (v. 10) uses a noun that means the process of dying, death-at-work, rather than the event. Paul is not saying that he dies as Jesus died, but that the same dying-of-Jesus that produced life for the world is at work in Paul’s ministry, producing life for the churches. The apostle’s weakness and suffering is the medium through which resurrection life is communicated. It is worth noting the honesty of v. 8: the verb behind “driven to despair” is the very word Paul used of himself in 1:8, where he says he despaired of life itself. He is describing the normal condition, not issuing an absolute guarantee.

Verse 13 — “I believed, and so I spoke” — quotes Psalm 116:10 in the Greek Old Testament, the psalm of a man who faced death and was delivered, who then declared that he believed and therefore spoke. Paul applies the psalm to the apostolic situation: even in the face of death, the minister speaks because he believes, and the faith of the psalmist and the faith of the Christian are shown to be one and the same pneuma. The resurrection of Jesus (v. 14) grounds this confidence — the same God who raised Jesus will raise us, and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor of a large church steps down due to a serious health diagnosis and is replaced by a younger, more energetic successor. He struggles with the sense that his fragility is a disqualification. This chapter is addressed precisely to him: the jar of clay is not a disqualification from ministry; it is the precondition for God’s power being unambiguously visible. The question is not whether his vessel is strong enough but whether the treasure is still present — and treasure in a cracked jar leaks light rather than hiding it.

verseByVerse.quote: But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we have this treasure in jars of clay, to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us.

But we have this treasure. Key words. The treasure: the light of the knowledge of God’s glory in Christ, the gospel (v. 6).

In jars of clay. Key words. Clay jars were cheap, fragile, everyday containers. Easily broken, easily replaced. Sometimes treasure was hidden in them, as in the Dead Sea Scrolls found in clay jars. The jars are human bodies and lives: weak, mortal, ordinary (Genesis 2:7; Isaiah 64:8).

To show that the surpassing power belongs to God and not to us. Key words. God deliberately puts his treasure in weak vessels so that no one confuses the power with the messenger. The weakness of the jar shows off the power of God.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness is good in itself. It means God uses weakness to display his strength (12:9).

In a sentence. But we have this treasure in clay jars, to show that this all-surpassing power is from God and not from us.

On a Tuesday. Do not be discouraged by your weakness. God has chosen to carry his treasure in a jar like you, so that his power shows.
verseByVerse.note: Clay jars were cheap, fragile, everyday containers.

verseByVerse.quote: We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed;

We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed. Key words. Four contrasts. “Afflicted” (thlibō, pressed, squeezed). “Not crushed” (stenochōreō, hemmed in, cornered with no space). Under pressure, but not trapped.

Perplexed, but not driven to despair. Key words. A wordplay: “perplexed” (aporoumenoi) but not “driven to despair” (exaporoumenoi): at a loss, but not utterly at a loss. Uncertain, but not hopeless. (In 1:8 Paul did despair of life; but not of God.)

Persecuted, but not forsaken. Key words. Hunted by enemies, but never abandoned by God (Hebrews 13:5).

Struck down, but not destroyed. Key words. Knocked to the ground, but not killed. Like a wrestler thrown but not beaten.

Where Christians differ: suffering and the prosperity gospel. Some teach that faith brings health, wealth and success, and that suffering shows weak faith. Verdict: The greatest apostle was constantly afflicted, perplexed, persecuted and struck down. Suffering is normal in the Christian life (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12). God’s promise is not to remove suffering but to sustain us in it and bring us through. The prosperity gospel contradicts the cross and the apostles’ experience.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians never feel crushed or despairing. It means they are never finally overcome.

In a sentence. We are hard pressed on every side, but not crushed; at a loss, but not in despair; persecuted, but not abandoned; knocked down, but not destroyed.

For worship. Read these lines as your own testimony. Thank God that he has not let you be crushed or forsaken.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay: “perplexed” (aporoumenoi) but not “driven to despair” (exaporoumenoi) — at a loss, but not utterly at a loss.

verseByVerse.quote: always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh.

Always carrying in the body the death of Jesus. Key words. “Death” (nekrōsis, dying, the process of being put to death). Paul’s sufferings for the gospel are a kind of ongoing dying, sharing Jesus’ sufferings (Galatians 6:17; Philippians 3:10).

So that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our bodies. Key words. The risen life of Jesus is seen in Paul’s survival, endurance and joy. The resurrection power of Christ shows itself in his weakness.

For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus’ sake. Key words. “Given over” (paradidōmi, handed over), the word used of Jesus being handed over to death. Paul is constantly handed over to danger.

So that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh. Key words. In mortal, dying flesh, the life of the risen Jesus becomes visible.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we must seek suffering. It means suffering for Christ’s sake displays his life.

In a sentence. We always carry around in our bodies the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our bodies. For we who are alive are always being handed over to death for Jesus’ sake, so that his life may be seen in our mortal bodies.

On a Tuesday. When following Jesus costs you something today, remember: his life is being shown through your dying.

verseByVerse.quote: So death is at work in us, but life in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So death is at work in us, but life in you.

So death is at work in us. Key words. The apostles suffer and are worn down.

But life in you. Key words. Their suffering brings spiritual life to the Corinthians. Like Christ, whose death brought life to others. Gospel ministry is costly: the minister spends himself so that others may live.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Corinthians should not suffer. They share in sufferings too (1:6–7). It means Paul’s suffering serves their life.

In a sentence. So death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.

For worship. Thank God for those who have spent themselves so that you could have life in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written, “I believed, and so I spoke,” we also believe, and so we also speak, knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and bring us with you into his presence.

Since we have the same spirit of faith according to what has been written. Key words. Paul shares the faith of the psalmist.

“I believed, and so I spoke.” Key words. Paul quotes the Greek form of the psalm (Psalm 116:10, Psalm 115:1 in the Greek). The psalmist, delivered from death, believed and spoke. Faith cannot stay silent.

We also believe, and so we also speak. Key words. Paul keeps preaching despite suffering, because he believes.

Knowing that he who raised the Lord Jesus will raise us also with Jesus. Key words. The resurrection is the ground of his courage. Even if he is killed, God will raise him.

And bring us with you into his presence. Key words. “Bring into his presence” (paristēmi, present). Paul and the Corinthians will stand together before God, raised and glorified.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only preachers should speak. All who believe should speak of Christ.

In a sentence. It is written, “I believed; therefore I have spoken.” With that same spirit of faith we also believe and therefore speak, because we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus from the dead will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you to himself.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, speak. The resurrection gives you courage to tell others about Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes the Greek form of the psalm.

parallels.desc: I believed, even when I spoke

verseByVerse.quote: For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is all for your sake, so that as grace extends to more and more people it may increase thanksgiving, to the glory of God.

For it is all for your sake. Key words. All Paul’s suffering and preaching is for the Corinthians’ benefit.

So that as grace extends to more and more people. Key words. Grace spreads as the gospel reaches more people.

It may increase thanksgiving. Key words. More people saved means more people giving thanks.

To the glory of God. Key words. The ultimate goal of everything: God’s glory. Ministry serves people, and people’s thanksgiving serves God’s glory.

What it does not mean. It does not mean people are only a means. God’s glory and people’s good go together.

In a sentence. All this is for your benefit, so that the grace reaching more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow to the glory of God.

For worship. Give thanks to God for his grace today. Your thanksgiving glorifies him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–18 — The Outer and Inner; the Seen and Unseen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So Paul does not lose heart. His body is wearing out, but his inner life is renewed daily. Present troubles, heavy as they are, are light and brief beside the lasting glory they are preparing. So he keeps his attention on what cannot yet be seen, because the visible things are temporary and the unseen ones eternal.
verseByVerse.theology: The seen/unseen contrast (v. 18) is not Platonic dualism — Paul is not saying that the material world is bad and the spiritual world is good, or that the body is a prison from which the soul escapes. He is making an eschatological point: what is currently visible (the suffering, the wasting body, the opposition) is temporary; what is currently invisible (the renewed inner person, the weight of glory being prepared) is permanent. The resurrection of the body (ch. 5; 1 Cor. 15) will make the invisible visible — the glory will become physical and permanent in the resurrection.
verseByVerse.examples: An elderly woman in a nursing home, her body failing, tells her pastor that she has never felt closer to God. She cannot explain it; the outer self is clearly wasting away. But there is something else. This verse names what she is experiencing: while the outer is being destroyed, the inner is being renewed day by day. The renewal is not despite the physical decline but somehow through it — the loosening grip of the outer on the inner’s attention, the daily reminder that this is not home, the intensified gaze at the unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.

So we do not lose heart. Key words. The same phrase as verse 1. Paul’s conclusion.

Though our outer self is wasting away. Key words. “Outer self” (literally outer man): the body and visible, earthly life, subject to aging, sickness, wear and suffering. “Wasting away” (diaphtheirō, decaying, being destroyed). Present tense: it is happening now.

Our inner self is being renewed day by day. Key words. “Inner self”: the inner person, the heart and spirit united to Christ. “Renewed” (anakainoō, made new). Daily, by the Spirit. As the body declines, the believer’s inner life can grow stronger (Colossians 3:10).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body does not matter. It will be raised (v. 14). It means its present decay is not the whole story.

In a sentence. Therefore we do not lose heart. Though outwardly we are wasting away, inwardly we are being renewed day by day.

On a Tuesday. As you grow older or weaker, ask God for daily inner renewal. Spend time with him each day.

verseByVerse.quote: For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison,

For this light momentary affliction. Key words. From a man who listed shipwrecks, beatings, imprisonment and near-death (11:23–27), an astonishing description: light and momentary. Not because it was easy, but because of what it is compared with.

Is preparing for us. Key words. “Preparing” (katergazomai, producing, working out). Suffering is not pointless. It is achieving something.

An eternal weight of glory. Key words. In Hebrew the word for “glory” (kabod) comes from a root meaning “heavy,” and Paul may be playing on this. Light affliction versus heavy glory; momentary versus eternal.

Beyond all comparison. Key words. Literally, according to excess unto excess: beyond all measure (Romans 8:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering earns glory. Glory is God’s gift. But suffering endured in faith prepares us for it.

In a sentence. For our light and brief troubles are achieving for us an eternal glory that far outweighs them all,

For worship. Put your present troubles on the scales against eternal glory. Thank God that glory far outweighs them.
verseByVerse.note: In Hebrew the word for “glory” comes from a root meaning “heavy” — glory has weight.

verseByVerse.quote: as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.

As we look not to the things that are seen. Key words. “Look” (skopeō, fix one’s eyes on, aim at). The secret of not losing heart: where you fix your gaze. Not on visible circumstances: sickness, opposition, loss.

But to the things that are unseen. Key words. God, Christ at his right hand, the resurrection, heaven (Hebrews 11:1, 27; 12:2).

For the things that are seen are transient. Key words. “Transient” (proskaira, temporary, for a season). Everything visible will pass.

But the things that are unseen are eternal. Key words. What cannot be seen will last forever.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring present realities or responsibilities. It means seeing them in eternal perspective.

In a sentence. So we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen, since what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.

On a Tuesday. Where are your eyes fixed today? Look up from your problems to the unseen and eternal.
