5.title: The Heavenly Dwelling, the Judgment Seat, and the Ministry of Reconciliation
5.overview:
Paul has just said that his outer self is wasting away and that he looks to what is unseen. Now he explains why death does not frighten him. If this tent, our present body, is taken down, we have a building from God, eternal in the heavens. We groan now, longing not to be stripped bare but to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life; and God has given the Spirit as a down payment. So Paul is courageous: he would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Either way, his aim is to please him, because all must appear before the judgement seat of Christ.

That fear of the Lord, and above all the love of Christ, drives his ministry. One died for all, so all died, so that the living should live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation. God has reconciled us to himself through Christ, not counting our sins against us, and has made Paul an ambassador with a message: be reconciled to God. The chapter ends with one of the greatest sentences in Scripture: God made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Heavenly Dwelling and the Judgment Seat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul explains why death does not frighten him. The present body is like a tent that will one day be taken down, but God has a permanent dwelling ready. Believers long to receive it, not to be left without a body but to have mortality swallowed up by life, and the Spirit is God’s guarantee. So Paul is confident: to leave the body is to be at home with the Lord, which he would prefer. Either way, his ambition is to please Christ, because everyone will stand before Christ’s judgement seat and give account for their life in the body.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment seat of Christ (v. 10) is a significant and sometimes neglected doctrine. Reformed theology insists on two distinct judgments: the justification that settles the believer’s eternal standing (entirely by grace, through faith, in Christ — Rom. 8:1: “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus”) and the assessment of the believer’s life and works (1 Cor. 3:10–15; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 22:12). At the bēma, salvation is not at stake; stewardship is. This distinction protects the gospel of grace while maintaining genuine accountability for the quality of the Christian life.
verseByVerse.examples: A Christian professional justifies a series of ethical compromises in his career with the thought that “grace covers everything.” He is not wrong about grace — but he is using it as a licence rather than a motivation. The judgment seat of Christ does not threaten his justification; it does call him to account for the quality of his stewardship. Paul says the knowledge of the judgment seat motivates him to “persuade others” (v. 11) — it is a motivating, not a threatening, reality for the justified believer.

verseByVerse.quote: For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 5 carries on from the unseen, eternal glory of 4:18 and then rises to the heart of the gospel. First, Paul speaks of death and the future. The present body is a tent that will be taken down; God has prepared a permanent building, the resurrection body. We groan now, longing not to be unclothed but to be clothed with life, and God has given the Spirit as a guarantee (vv. 1–5). So we are of good courage: to be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord. Whether here or there, we aim to please him, for all will appear before the judgement seat of Christ (vv. 6–10). Second, Paul explains what drives his ministry: the fear of the Lord and the love of Christ. One died for all, so that those who live might live for him. Anyone in Christ is a new creation (vv. 11–17). Third, the message itself: God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, not counting trespasses. So we are ambassadors, pleading: be reconciled to God. For God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (vv. 18–21). Verse 21 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of the great exchange at the heart of the gospel.

For we know that if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed. Key words. Paul, a tentmaker by trade, pictures the present body as a tent: temporary, fragile, easily taken down (2 Peter 1:13–14). “Destroyed” (katalyō, taken down, dismantled): death.

We have a building from God. Key words. In contrast to a tent, a solid building, permanent. From God: his work.

A house not made with hands. Key words. Not human-made, but God-made (Mark 14:58; Hebrews 9:11).

Eternal in the heavens. Key words. Permanent, prepared in heaven now, to be given at the resurrection. Most take this as the resurrection body (1 Corinthians 15:42–54). We have it: it is so certain it can be spoken of as present.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we receive the resurrection body at the moment of death. The resurrection happens at Christ’s return (1 Corinthians 15:52). Between death and resurrection, the soul is with the Lord (v. 8).

In a sentence. For we know that if the earthly tent we live in is taken down, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands.

On a Tuesday. Your body is a tent. Care for it, but do not cling to it. A better home is waiting.
verseByVerse.note: Paul, a tentmaker by trade, pictures the present body as a tent — temporary — and the resurrection body as a permanent building.

parallels.desc: houses of clay

verseByVerse.quote: For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling, if indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked.

For in this tent we groan. Key words. “Groan” (stenazō): the sigh of suffering and longing (Romans 8:23). Life in the present body involves pain and weakness.

Longing to put on our heavenly dwelling. Key words. Paul mixes metaphors: building and clothing. He longs to be clothed with the resurrection body.

If indeed by putting it on we may not be found naked. Key words. Naked: without a body, a disembodied spirit. Greeks thought being free of the body was ideal. Paul does not. A bodiless state is not the goal; resurrection is. Some manuscripts read “taking it off” instead of “putting it on”; the ESV note mentions this.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the soul without the body is unhappy. Being with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:23). But it is incomplete until resurrection.

In a sentence. Meanwhile we groan, longing to be clothed with our heavenly dwelling, because when we are clothed we will not be found without a body.

For worship. If you groan in your body, bring it to God. Tell him you long for resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened—not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

For while we are still in this tent, we groan, being burdened. Key words. “Burdened” (bareō, weighed down), as in 1:8.

Not that we would be unclothed. Key words. Paul does not long for death itself, the stripping off of the body.

But that we would be further clothed. Key words. “Further clothed” (ependyomai, put on over). He would prefer to be alive at Christ’s return and have the resurrection body put on over the present one, without dying (1 Corinthians 15:51–53).

So that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. Key words. As death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54), mortality will be swallowed by life.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul feared death. He longed for the fullness of life, which only resurrection brings.

In a sentence. For while we are in this tent, we groan and are burdened, not because we want to be unclothed but to be clothed over with our heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

On a Tuesday. Death is not the goal; life is. Hold onto the hope of resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee.

He who has prepared us for this very thing is God. Key words. “Prepared” (katergazomai, fashioned, made ready). God designed us for resurrection glory. This is our destiny.

Who has given us the Spirit as a guarantee. Key words. The word for “guarantee” (arrabōn) was used for a deposit or first instalment (1:22; Ephesians 1:14). The Spirit is the first part of our future life, given now, guaranteeing the rest. The Spirit who raised Jesus will raise us (Romans 8:11).

What it does not mean. It does not mean resurrection is uncertain. The deposit guarantees it.

In a sentence. Now the one who has fashioned us for this very purpose is God, who has given us the Spirit as a deposit, guaranteeing what is to come.

For worship. The Spirit in you is God’s down payment on your resurrection. Thank him for that pledge.
verseByVerse.note: The word for “guarantee” was used for a deposit or first instalment, pledging full payment later.

verseByVerse.quote: So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So we are always of good courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord, for we walk by faith, not by sight.

So we are always of good courage. Key words. “Of good courage” (tharreō, confident, cheerful). Because of the Spirit’s guarantee.

We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. Key words. “At home” (endēmeō) and “away” (ekdēmeō): living in a country and being abroad. In this life we are with Christ by the Spirit, but not yet face to face.

For we walk by faith, not by sight. Key words. Now we trust what we cannot see. One day faith will become sight (1 Corinthians 13:12; 1 Peter 1:8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ is absent from believers now. He is with us (Matthew 28:20). But not visibly.

In a sentence. Therefore we are always confident, knowing that as long as we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord. For we live by faith, not by sight.

On a Tuesday. Walk by faith today. Trust what God has said, even when you cannot see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yes, we are of good courage, and we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

Yes, we are of good courage. Key words. Repeated.

And we would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord. Key words. At death, the believer leaves the body and goes immediately home to the Lord. This is the intermediate state: between death and resurrection, the soul is consciously with Christ (Philippians 1:23; Luke 23:43). Paul prefers that to this life, though he would most prefer the resurrection.

Where Christians differ: what happens at death? Some teach soul sleep, an unconscious state until the resurrection; Roman Catholics teach purgatory for most believers. Verdict: To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord, immediately and consciously. There is no purgatory and no soul sleep. The souls of believers, made perfect in holiness, are received into heaven, where they behold God’s face in light and glory, waiting for the full redemption of their bodies (Westminster 32.1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should seek death. It means they need not fear it.

In a sentence. We are confident, and would prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

For worship. If someone you love has died in Christ, they are at home with the Lord. Thank God for that comfort.

verseByVerse.quote: So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil.

So whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. Key words. “Make it our aim” (philotimeomai, aspire, strive ambitiously). Paul’s great ambition: to please Christ, in life or death.

For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ. Key words. The judgement seat (bēma) was the raised platform where a Roman official judged cases. Paul had stood before one in Corinth (Acts 18:12). “Appear” (phaneroō, be made manifest, laid open). Our lives will be fully exposed.

So that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body. Key words. Our deeds in this bodily life matter forever.

Whether good or evil. Key words. All deeds will be assessed.

Where Christians differ: judgement of believers. How can believers, who are justified and free from condemnation (Romans 8:1), be judged by their works? Verdict: Believers will not be condemned; their sins are covered by Christ. But their lives will be revealed and evaluated, and their works rewarded according to God’s grace (1 Corinthians 3:12–15; Matthew 25:21). Good works do not earn justification, but they are the evidence of true faith, and God graciously rewards them (Westminster 33.1). The judgement will also openly vindicate God’s people and show his justice.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on our works. It means our works matter.

In a sentence. So whether we are at home in the body or away from it, our aim is to please him. For we must all appear before the judgement seat of Christ, so that each of us may receive what is due for what we have done in the body, good or bad.

On a Tuesday. Make it your ambition today to please Christ. You will give an account of how you lived.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat (bema) was the raised platform where a Roman official gave judgment; Paul had stood before one in Corinth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — The Ministry of Reconciliation and the Great Exchange
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Knowing the fear of the Lord, Paul tries to persuade people, and he hopes the Corinthians can see his sincerity and answer those who boast in appearances. What drives him is Christ’s love: one died for all, so all who are his have died with him and now live for him. Paul no longer judges anyone, Christ included, by worldly standards; whoever is in Christ belongs to the new creation. God has reconciled people to himself through Christ, not counting their sins against them, and has made Paul his envoy, pleading with people to accept that reconciliation. The ground of it all is an exchange: the sinless Christ was treated as sin for us, so that in him we might be counted righteous before God.
verseByVerse.theology:
“In Christ God was reconciling the world to himself” (v. 19) — the agency is God’s. Reconciliation is initiated, accomplished, and offered by God, not by humanity. The word order matters and is often misquoted: it is not that God was waiting to be reconciled to humanity, as if he needed to be persuaded or appeased by a more merciful Son. Rather, God himself was the reconciler — the one who, in Christ, removed the obstacle that prevented humanity from being reconciled to him. The obstacle is sin; the removal is the cross, and v. 21 states its cost.

Verse 21 — “he made him to be sin who knew no sin” — requires precise handling. “Made him to be sin” does not mean Christ became a sinner or had sinful desires. It means God treated Christ as the sin-bearer — the one who stood in the place of sinners, receiving the judgment that sin deserves. The Old Testament background is the sin offering: in Leviticus the offering itself is called by the same word as the sin it carried, the animal becoming the sin-bearer, and Isaiah says it without a picture at all — “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa. 53:6). The result: we “become the righteousness of God” — not merely receive a righteous verdict but are constituted righteous in him, which is why the standing cannot be damaged by a bad week.
verseByVerse.examples: An evangelism trainer teaches his church that the goal of evangelism is to persuade people to make a decision for Christ. This passage suggests a deeper framework: the goal is to implore people, on Christ’s behalf, to be reconciled to God — as ambassadors of a reconciliation that God himself has already accomplished and is already offering. The difference is not merely semantic: the ambassador does not create the peace; he announces and conveys the peace that the King has already made.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us, so that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart.

Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. Key words. The fear of the Lord: reverent awe before the Judge (v. 10). Because Paul knows people will face judgement, he persuades (peithō), reasons with them, pleads (Acts 17:4; 18:4).

But what we are is known to God. Key words. “Known” (phaneroō, made manifest). God sees Paul’s heart completely.

And I hope it is known also to your conscience. Key words. Paul hopes the Corinthians, in their consciences, recognise his sincerity.

We are not commending ourselves to you again but giving you cause to boast about us. Key words. He is giving them material to defend him against his critics.

So that you may be able to answer those who boast about outward appearance and not about what is in the heart. Key words. The rival teachers boasted of impressive externals: eloquence, credentials, visions. Paul cares about the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean evangelism should be driven by fear tactics. It means the reality of judgement makes evangelism urgent.

In a sentence. Since we know what it is to fear the Lord, we try to persuade others. What we are is plain to God, and Paul hopes it is plain to your conscience too. We are not commending ourselves again, but giving you reason to be proud of us, so that you can answer those who take pride in appearance rather than in what is in the heart.

For worship. Ask God for a holy fear of him that makes you eager to persuade others about Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.

For if we are beside ourselves, it is for God. Key words. “Beside ourselves” (existēmi, out of one’s mind). Some accused Paul of being crazy, perhaps because of his zeal, or his ecstatic experiences (12:1–4; Acts 26:24). If so, that is between him and God.

If we are in our right mind, it is for you. Key words. “Right mind” (sōphroneō, sober, sensible). When he teaches soberly and clearly, it is for their benefit. Either way, his life is not for himself.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was unstable. It means everything he did was for God and others.

In a sentence. If we are out of our mind, as some say, it is for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.

On a Tuesday. Do not be afraid of looking foolish for God. And when you speak to others, speak sensibly for their good.

verseByVerse.quote: For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the love of Christ controls us, because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died; and he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised.

For the love of Christ controls us. Key words. The love of Christ: his love for us, shown at the cross. “Controls” (synechō, hems in, compels, presses on all sides, like a river between banks). Christ’s love is the driving force of Paul’s life.

Because we have concluded this: that one has died for all, therefore all have died. Key words. One died for all: Christ died as the representative and substitute of his people. Therefore all have died: when he died, they died with him, in union with him (Romans 6:3–8; Galatians 2:20). His death counts as theirs.

And he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves. Key words. Those who live: those who now have new life in Christ. His death frees them from self-centred living.

But for him who for their sake died and was raised. Key words. The new life is lived for Christ. The cross and resurrection change the direction of a life.

Where Christians differ: for whom did Christ die? Some take “all” here to mean that Christ died for every human being equally, making salvation possible for all. Verdict: Paul says the all for whom Christ died have died with him, and live for him. That describes those united to Christ, not every human. Christ died effectively for all his people, of every nation, securing their salvation, not merely making it possible (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). This is definite atonement. The gospel is offered sincerely to every person, and Christ’s death is sufficient for all, but it was designed to save his people (Canons of Dort 2.3, 8).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s love is limited in its sincerity. His love for his people is infinite. And the gospel call goes to all.

In a sentence. For Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that one died for all, and therefore all died. And he died for all, so that those who live should no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them and was raised again.

For worship. Let the love of Christ press on you today. Live not for yourself, but for him who died and rose for you.

verseByVerse.quote: From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh, we regard him thus no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come.

From now on, therefore, we regard no one according to the flesh. Key words. According to the flesh: by worldly standards: appearance, status, ethnicity, success. The cross changes how we see everyone.

Even though we once regarded Christ according to the flesh. Key words. Before his conversion, Paul judged Jesus by worldly standards: a crucified failure, cursed by God.

We regard him thus no longer. Key words. Now he sees Christ as the risen Lord.

Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. Key words. “New creation” (kainē ktisis). Literally: if anyone is in Christ, new creation! Not just a new person, but part of God’s new creation, the age to come breaking in (Isaiah 65:17; Galatians 6:15). Conversion is creation, not renovation.

The old has passed away; behold, the new has come. Key words. Echoes Isaiah 43:18–19: remember not the former things; behold, I am doing a new thing. The old order of sin and death is passing; the new has arrived in Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never sin or struggle. The old nature still fights (Galatians 5:17). But the believer’s identity is new.

In a sentence. So from now on we regard no one from a worldly point of view. Though we once regarded Christ that way, we do so no longer. Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, the new creation has come: the old has gone, the new is here!

On a Tuesday. You are a new creation. Do not let your past define you. And look at others, not by worldly standards, but as people for whom Christ died.

parallels.desc: behold, I am doing a new thing

verseByVerse.quote: All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All this is from God, who through Christ reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation.

All this is from God. Key words. The new creation is God’s work, from start to finish.

Who through Christ reconciled us to himself. Key words. “Reconciled” (katallassō, changed from enmity to friendship). We were God’s enemies (Romans 5:10). God took the initiative. Notice: God reconciled us to himself. The barrier was on both sides: our rebellion, and God’s just wrath. Christ removed both.

And gave us the ministry of reconciliation. Key words. The task of proclaiming it.

That is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself. Key words. The world: people from every nation, not just Israel. God acted in Christ for a world in rebellion.

Not counting their trespasses against them. Key words. “Counting” (logizomai, reckoning, crediting). God does not put sins on the account of those reconciled, because he put them on Christ (v. 21; Romans 4:8).

And entrusting to us the message of reconciliation. Key words. God placed this message in his messengers’ hands.

Where Christians differ: is the whole world reconciled? Universalists read this as saying every person is already reconciled. Verdict: If everyone were already reconciled, Paul would not need to plead: be reconciled to God (v. 20). God accomplished reconciliation in Christ for the world of his people from every nation, and it is received by faith. The message goes to all, calling all to receive it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God needed to be persuaded to love us. His love sent Christ. But his justice needed to be satisfied, and Christ satisfied it.

In a sentence. All this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that God was reconciling the world to himself in Christ, not counting people’s sins against them. And he has committed to us the message of reconciliation.

For worship. You were God’s enemy, and he made you his friend. Praise him for reconciling you to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, God making his appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ. Key words. An ambassador (presbeuō) spoke with the authority of the king who sent him, carrying his message exactly. Paul represents Christ.

God making his appeal through us. Key words. When the gospel is preached, God himself is pleading. “Appeal” (parakaleō, urge, beg).

We implore you on behalf of Christ. Key words. “Implore” (deomai, beg, plead). The tone of the gospel is not cold command but urgent pleading.

Be reconciled to God. Key words. Accept the reconciliation God has provided. Stop fighting him. Receive his peace. Even to the Corinthian believers, Paul calls them to live out reconciliation, perhaps because some were drifting.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we reconcile ourselves by effort. It means we receive what God has done.

In a sentence. So we are Christ’s ambassadors, as though God were making his appeal through us. We beg you on Christ’s behalf: be reconciled to God.

On a Tuesday. You are Christ’s ambassador at work, at home, with friends. Carry his message of peace faithfully.
verseByVerse.note: An ambassador spoke with the authority of the king who sent him.

verseByVerse.quote: For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

For our sake he made him to be sin. Key words. God the Father made Christ to be sin. Not that Christ became sinful, but that God treated him as sin, laid our sins on him, and punished sin in him (Isaiah 53:6, 10; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24). Some understand the word here to mean a sin offering, as it sometimes does in the Greek translation of Leviticus 4. Either way, he bore our sin.

Who knew no sin. Key words. Christ was sinless (Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22; 1 John 3:5). Only a sinless one could bear others’ sin.

So that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Key words. The great exchange. He took our sin; we receive his righteousness. In him: through union with Christ. The righteousness of God: the right standing God gives, credited to us (Romans 3:21–22; Philippians 3:9). As Christ was treated as a sinner though he was not, we are treated as righteous though we are not.

Where Christians differ: imputation. Some deny that our sin was legally credited to Christ and his righteousness legally credited to us, saying instead that we are made righteous only by inner transformation. Verdict: The parallel is exact. Christ was made sin, not by becoming sinful inside, but by having our sin counted to him. So we become righteous, not first by inner change, but by having his righteousness counted to us. This is double imputation, the heart of justification by faith alone (Westminster 11.1; Heidelberg Catechism Q. 60). Inner transformation follows in sanctification, but it is not the ground of our acceptance with God. And it shows the cross as penal substitution.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ ever stopped being holy, or that God the Father hated the Son. Christ was beloved even as he bore the Father’s wrath against sin.

In a sentence. God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

For worship. Meditate on the great exchange: your sin on him, his righteousness on you. Then worship.

parallels.desc: he was pierced for our transgressions

6.title: The Open Heart, the Catalogue of Hardships, and the Unequal Yoke
6.overview:
Having said that God makes his appeal through his ambassadors, Paul makes it: do not receive God’s grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation. Then he shows the Corinthians what a true servant of God looks like, in one of the most powerful passages he ever wrote. It is not a list of successes but of endurance: beatings, prisons, riots, sleepless nights and hunger, and alongside them purity, kindness, the Holy Spirit and genuine love. He lives in paradoxes: treated as an impostor yet true, dying yet alive, sorrowful yet always rejoicing, poor yet making many rich, having nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart wide to them; he asks them to open theirs.

Then a sudden, sharp section (6:14–7:1): do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Light has nothing in common with darkness, nor Christ with Belial, nor God’s temple with idols. The church is the temple of the living God, as the prophets promised, so it must come out and be separate from idolatry and impurity, and God will be a Father to his sons and daughters.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Open Heart and the Catalogue of Hardships
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s fellow workers, Paul urges the Corinthians not to let God’s grace come to nothing in them: the time of God’s favour that Isaiah promised has arrived. He takes care that his conduct puts no obstacle in anyone’s way. His credentials are not successes but endurance in hardship, beatings, prison, riots, overwork and hunger, together with purity, patience, kindness, the Spirit, love and truthful speech. His life is full of paradox: dishonoured yet honoured, called a fraud yet genuine, dying yet alive, grieving yet always glad, poor yet enriching many, owning nothing yet possessing everything. He has opened his heart to them and asks them to open theirs in return.
verseByVerse.theology: The catalogue of hardships (vv. 4–5) is one of several in 2 Corinthians (cf. 4:8–9; 11:23–29; 12:10). Together they constitute Paul’s theology of the cross applied to ministry: the authentic apostle is identified not by spectacular results or impressive presence but by the pattern of cruciform suffering. This does not glorify suffering for its own sake; it identifies the shape that kingdom advance takes in a world that crucified its King. Those who carry the message of the cross will bear in their bodies the pattern of the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: A young minister enters a hard urban church plant with ambitions of rapid growth and visible impact. After three years, he has a small congregation, many failures, and a life that looks more like Paul’s catalogue than his vision board. He questions his calling. This passage is the specific word for him: the catalogue of hardships is not evidence of failed ministry but of authentic ministry. The question is not whether ministry is fruitful by visible metrics but whether the minister is conducting himself with the character described in vv. 6–7.

verseByVerse.quote: Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Working together with him, then, we appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 6 continues Paul’s appeal from 5:20. First, he urges the Corinthians not to receive God’s grace in vain, for now is the day of salvation (vv. 1–2). Second, he describes his ministry, to show that it gives no one cause to stumble: through endurance in every kind of hardship, through the fruit of the Spirit, through honour and dishonour, appearing as an impostor, dying, sorrowful and poor, yet true, alive, rejoicing, and making many rich (vv. 3–10). Third, he opens his heart to them and asks them to open theirs in return (vv. 11–13). Finally, he warns them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Light and darkness, Christ and Belial, the temple of God and idols cannot be partners. We are the temple of the living God, so come out and be separate, and God will be our Father (6:14–7:1).

Working together with him, then. Key words. “Working together” (synergeō). Paul works with God, as God’s fellow worker (1 Corinthians 3:9), in the ministry of reconciliation.

We appeal to you not to receive the grace of God in vain. Key words. “In vain” (eis kenon, to emptiness). Do not let God’s grace be wasted on you. Some Corinthians were in danger of drifting after false teachers (11:3–4) and unholy living (12:21).

For he says, “In a favorable time I listened to you, and in a day of salvation I have helped you.” Key words. From Isaiah 49:8, God’s word to his servant, promising salvation and the restoration of his people.

Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation. Key words. The day Isaiah foresaw has arrived in Christ. Now is the time to respond. Do not delay (Hebrews 3:7–8, 13).

What it does not mean. It does not mean true believers can lose their salvation. It means that professing believers must show that grace has truly taken hold, and that the call to respond is urgent.

In a sentence. As God’s co-workers we urge you not to receive God’s grace in vain. For he says, “At the right time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” Now is the right time; now is the day of salvation.

On a Tuesday. Is there a step of obedience you have been putting off? Today is the day. Do not waste God’s grace.

parallels.desc: in a time of favour I have answered you

verseByVerse.quote: We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We put no obstacle in anyone’s way, so that no fault may be found with our ministry,

We put no obstacle in anyone’s way. Key words. “Obstacle” (proskopē, something to stumble over). Paul tried never to give anyone a reason to reject the gospel because of his conduct (1 Corinthians 9:12; 10:32).

So that no fault may be found with our ministry. Key words. “Fault” (mōmaomai, blame, ridicule). He guards the ministry’s reputation, because it represents Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean avoiding the offence of the gospel itself. The cross offends; the messenger should not add offence.

In a sentence. We put no stumbling block in anyone’s path, so that our ministry will not be discredited.

For worship. Pray that your life will never be the reason someone rejects Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;
verseByVerse.commentary:
but as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, hardships, calamities, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, sleepless nights, hunger;

But as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way. Key words. Paul’s credentials are not letters but a life (3:1). “Servants” (diakonoi).

By great endurance. Key words. “Endurance” (hypomonē, staying power). The heading for what follows.

In afflictions, hardships, calamities. Key words. Three general troubles: pressures (thlipseis), hardships (anankai, necessities, constraints), calamities (stenochōriai, tight places, distresses).

Beatings, imprisonments, riots. Key words. Three troubles from others. Paul was beaten many times (11:23–25; Acts 16:22–23), imprisoned (Acts 16:23), and faced riots (Acts 14:19; 19:29).

Labors, sleepless nights, hunger. Key words. Three self-chosen hardships: hard work, lost sleep, going without food, for the gospel’s sake (1 Thessalonians 2:9).

What it does not mean. It does not mean suffering proves a ministry is true. False teachers can suffer too. But true ministry is marked by endurance in suffering, not escape from it.

In a sentence. Rather, as servants of God we commend ourselves in every way: in great endurance; in troubles, hardships and distresses; in beatings, imprisonments and riots; in hard work, sleepless nights and hunger;

On a Tuesday. Pray for persecuted Christians who know these hardships today. Ask God to give them endurance.

verseByVerse.quote: by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;
verseByVerse.commentary:
by purity, knowledge, patience, kindness, the Holy Spirit, genuine love; by truthful speech, and the power of God; with the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left;

By purity, knowledge, patience, kindness. Key words. Now inner qualities. Purity (hagnotēs, moral cleanness, sincerity). Knowledge: of the gospel. Patience (makrothymia, long-suffering). Kindness (chrēstotēs). Compare the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22).

The Holy Spirit. Key words. The source of all these qualities. Some take it as a holy spirit, a holy attitude, but the Holy Spirit fits best.

Genuine love. Key words. “Genuine” (anypokritos, unhypocritical, Romans 12:9).

By truthful speech, and the power of God. Key words. The word of truth: the gospel, and honest speech. The power of God: the Spirit working through it.

With the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left. Key words. Weapons “for the right hand and for the left” are weapons for attack and defence: a sword in the right hand and a shield in the left. Righteousness: right living and the righteousness of God in Christ (Ephesians 6:14–17). Paul’s weapons are spiritual and moral, not manipulation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was perfect in all of these. It means they characterised his ministry.

In a sentence. in purity, understanding, patience and kindness; in the Holy Spirit and in sincere love; in truthful speech and in the power of God; with weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left;

For worship. Ask the Holy Spirit to produce in you purity, patience, kindness and genuine love.
verseByVerse.note: Weapons “for the right hand and for the left” are weapons for attack (the sword) and defence (the shield).

verseByVerse.quote: through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;
verseByVerse.commentary:
through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. We are treated as impostors, and yet are true; as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and behold, we live; as punished, and yet not killed;

Through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise. Key words. Paul’s ministry goes on whether people praise or insult him. He is not controlled by reputation.

We are treated as impostors, and yet are true. Key words. A series of paradoxes. “Impostors” (planoi, deceivers): what his opponents called him, as Jesus’ enemies called him (Matthew 27:63). Yet Paul is true.

As unknown, and yet well known. Key words. Unknown and insignificant to the world; known to God and to the churches.

As dying, and behold, we live. Key words. Always near death, yet kept alive (4:10–11).

As punished, and yet not killed. Key words. “Punished” (paideuō, disciplined, chastened). Echoes Psalm 118:18: the LORD has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the world’s view is unimportant. It means God’s view is what counts.

In a sentence. through glory and dishonour, bad report and good report; genuine, yet regarded as impostors; known, yet regarded as unknown; dying, and yet we live on; beaten, and yet not killed;

On a Tuesday. When people misjudge you for following Christ, remember: God knows you, and his verdict stands.

verseByVerse.quote: as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.

As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing. Key words. Real sorrow, over sin, suffering and the lost (Romans 9:2), and constant joy in the Lord (Philippians 4:4). Both at once. Christian joy is not the absence of sorrow but something deeper underneath it.

As poor, yet making many rich. Key words. Paul had little money, but enriched many with the gospel, as Christ became poor to make us rich (8:9).

As having nothing, yet possessing everything. Key words. No possessions, but owner of all things in Christ (1 Corinthians 3:21–23; Romans 8:32). The Christian is the richest person in the world.

What it does not mean. It does not mean poverty is holier than wealth. It means riches in Christ outweigh all earthly wealth.

In a sentence. sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; poor, yet making many rich; having nothing, and yet possessing everything.

For worship. Even in sorrow, rejoice in the Lord. Even with little, thank him that in Christ you possess everything.

verseByVerse.quote: We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians; our heart is wide open. You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own affections.

We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians. Key words. Literally, our mouth is open to you. Paul has spoken frankly and fully. He uses their name, the only time he addresses them directly as Corinthians, a sign of deep emotion.

Our heart is wide open. Key words. “Wide open” (platynō, enlarged). His heart has room for all of them.

You are not restricted by us. Key words. “Restricted” (stenochōreō, cramped, squeezed). Paul has not closed his heart to them.

But you are restricted in your own affections. Key words. “Affections” (splanchna, the inner organs, the seat of feelings). The problem is their narrow hearts toward him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sentimental. He was honestly asking for reconciliation.

In a sentence. We have spoken freely to you, Corinthians, and opened wide our hearts to you. We are not withholding our affection from you, but you are withholding yours from us.

On a Tuesday. Is your heart narrow toward someone who loves you? Open it.

verseByVerse.quote: In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In return (I speak as to children) widen your hearts also.

In return (I speak as to children). Key words. As a father to his children (1 Corinthians 4:14–15).

Widen your hearts also. Key words. Love me back. Make room for me in your hearts. Reconciliation needs both sides.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul needed their approval for his ministry. He wanted their love for their own good and his joy.

In a sentence. As a fair exchange (Paul speaks as to his children), open wide your hearts also.

For worship. Ask God to enlarge your heart toward the people he has given you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–7:1 — Do Not Be Unequally Yoked
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to bind themselves in partnerships with unbelievers that compromise their loyalty to Christ. Righteousness and lawlessness, light and darkness, Christ and Satan, God’s temple and idols have nothing in common. The church is God’s temple, the place where he has promised to live among his people. So, drawing on several prophetic promises, Paul calls them to leave idolatry and impurity behind, and God will welcome them as his sons and daughters. Holding such promises, they should cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit and pursue holiness in reverence for God.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage has been applied to several specific situations: (1) Marriage between believers and unbelievers — the most common application, supported by the principle if not the primary context. 1 Cor. 7:39 (she is free to marry “only in the Lord”) is the direct marriage prohibition. (2) Formal religious partnerships — interfaith worship, ecumenical agreements that require treating fundamental doctrinal differences as unimportant. (3) Business partnerships that require ethical compromise. The principle is: any relationship of primary spiritual allegiance that requires pulling in the same direction as one who is opposed to Christ creates an incompatible yoke. Ordinary friendship, working relationships, and engagement with unbelievers are not in view — Paul explicitly says in 1 Cor. 5:9–10 that he did not mean to avoid all contact with the immoral of the world.
verseByVerse.examples: A senior pastor receives an invitation to co-host a community prayer service with leaders from several faiths, including those who explicitly deny the Trinity and the uniqueness of Christ as Saviour. He must decide whether this is a civic engagement (speaking to the community) or a spiritual partnership (worshipping together). This passage suggests the distinction matters: representing the church’s concern for the community is different from implying that all faith traditions are pulling the same spiritual yoke toward the same God.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?

Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. Key words. “Unequally yoked” (heterozygeō, yoked with a different kind). The picture comes from the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to plough together (Deuteronomy 22:10). They pull differently and cannot work together. Believers should not be bound in close partnerships that join them to unbelievers in ways that compromise their faith.

For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Key words. Five rhetorical questions, each expecting the answer: none. Partnership (metochē, sharing).

Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Key words. Fellowship (koinōnia). Light and darkness are opposites (John 3:19–21; Ephesians 5:8–11).

Where Christians differ: what is an unequal yoke? Some apply this only to marriage; others to any contact with unbelievers. Verdict: In context, Paul’s main concern is probably Corinthians joining in pagan temple worship and following false teachers. The principle applies to any binding partnership that pulls a believer away from Christ: most clearly marriage (1 Corinthians 7:39), and also business partnerships or alliances that compromise faith and obedience. It does not forbid friendship, work or ordinary life with unbelievers, which Paul assumes (1 Corinthians 5:10; 10:27).

What it does not mean. It does not mean a believer already married to an unbeliever should leave (1 Corinthians 7:12–13). It means do not enter such a yoke.

In a sentence. Do not be yoked together with unbelievers. For what do righteousness and wickedness have in common? Or what fellowship can light have with darkness?

On a Tuesday. Before you enter any binding commitment, a marriage, business, or alliance, ask: will this pull me with Christ, or against him?
verseByVerse.note: The picture comes from the law forbidding an ox and a donkey to be yoked together at the plough.

verseByVerse.quote: What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?
verseByVerse.commentary:
What accord has Christ with Belial? Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever?

What accord has Christ with Belial? Key words. Belial (“worthlessness”) was a Jewish name for Satan, used in the Dead Sea Scrolls. “Accord” (symphōnēsis, harmony, from which symphony). Christ and Satan cannot sing together.

Or what portion does a believer share with an unbeliever? Key words. “Portion” (meris, share, part). In the deepest things, believers and unbelievers have no common share. Their destinies differ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers are better people. It means they belong to a different kingdom.

In a sentence. What harmony is there between Christ and Belial? Or what does a believer have in common with an unbeliever?

For worship. Thank God that you belong to Christ, not to Belial. Live in harmony with your Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Belial (“worthlessness”) was a Jewish name for Satan.

verseByVerse.quote: What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; as God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.

What agreement has the temple of God with idols? Key words. “Agreement” (synkatathesis, a joint decision). Idols in God’s temple were the ultimate sacrilege (2 Kings 21:4–7; Ezekiel 8).

For we are the temple of the living God. Key words. The church is God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16). So it cannot join itself to idol worship.

As God said, “I will make my dwelling among them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” Key words. Paul combines Leviticus 26:11–12 and Ezekiel 37:27. The heart of the covenant: God living among his people. Now fulfilled in the church, by the Spirit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s presence is limited to church buildings. His people are the temple.

In a sentence. What agreement is there between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God. As God has said: “I will live with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

On a Tuesday. You are part of God’s temple. Keep your life free of idols.

parallels.desc: I will walk among you and be your God

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord, and touch no unclean thing; then I will welcome you,

Therefore go out from their midst, and be separate from them, says the Lord. Key words. From Isaiah 52:11, God’s call to the exiles to leave Babylon, carrying the temple vessels. Believers must separate themselves from idolatry and the corrupting practices of the world.

And touch no unclean thing. Key words. Moral and spiritual uncleanness, now, rather than ritual.

Then I will welcome you. Key words. From Ezekiel 20:34. God receives those who come out from idolatry.

Where Christians differ: separation. Some interpret separation as withdrawing from all association with the world, or even from other Christians who associate with unbelievers. Verdict: Separation here means refusing to take part in idolatry and sin, not physical withdrawal from the world (John 17:15; 1 Corinthians 5:9–10). Christians are to be in the world but not of it. Separating from other true believers over secondary matters is not what Paul teaches; he calls for separation from false worship and from those who teach a false gospel (Galatians 1:8–9; Romans 16:17).

What it does not mean. It does not mean God only welcomes us after we have cleaned ourselves up. He welcomes sinners. But those he welcomes leave their idols.

In a sentence. Therefore, “Come out from them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.”

For worship. Is there something unclean you need to leave behind? Leave it, and run to the God who welcomes you.

parallels.desc: depart, go out from there; touch no unclean thing

verseByVerse.quote: and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me, says the Lord Almighty.”

And I will be a father to you. Key words. From 2 Samuel 7:14, God’s promise to David’s son. Paul applies it to all believers.

And you shall be sons and daughters to me. Key words. Paul adds “and daughters” (echoing Isaiah 43:6). Women are fully God’s children, equal heirs of the promise. Adoption into God’s family (Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:5–7).

Says the Lord Almighty. Key words. “Almighty” (pantokratōr, ruler of all). The Almighty becomes our Father. The greatest privilege imaginable.

What it does not mean. It does not mean adoption is earned by separation. It is God’s gracious gift, which calls us to holy living.

In a sentence. And, “I will be a Father to you, and you will be my sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.”

On a Tuesday. The Lord Almighty is your Father. Live today as his son or daughter, secure and loved.

parallels.desc: I will be to him a father
bring my sons and my daughters

7.title: Godly Grief and the Joy of Reconciliation
7.overview:
Chapter 7 finishes two things. First, the call to holiness: since God has promised to live among his people and be their Father, they must cleanse themselves from everything that defiles body and spirit (7:1). Second, the story Paul broke off at 2:13. He had left Troas in anxiety and gone into Macedonia, where he found no rest: fighting outside, fear inside. Then Titus arrived with news from Corinth. The severe letter had hurt them, but the hurt had led to repentance. They had grieved, longed for Paul, and dealt with the offender.

So Paul explains the difference between two kinds of sorrow. Godly grief produces repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret; worldly grief produces death. He lists what their godly grief produced: earnestness, eagerness to clear themselves, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and readiness to see justice done. Titus has been refreshed by them, Paul’s boasting about them has proved true, and he rejoices that he can have complete confidence in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since we have these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God.

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 7 brings the long defence of Paul’s ministry (2:14–7:4) to a close and returns to the story of Titus. Verse 1 concludes the call to separation in chapter 6: since God has promised to dwell among us and be our Father, let us cleanse ourselves and pursue holiness. Then Paul asks again for open hearts (vv. 2–4). He tells how, in Macedonia, harassed and afraid, he was comforted by the arrival of Titus with news that the Corinthians had responded to his severe letter with grief, longing and zeal (vv. 5–7). He does not regret the letter, because their grief was godly grief, which leads to repentance and salvation, unlike worldly grief, which leads to death. He describes the marks of their repentance: earnestness, eagerness to put things right, indignation, fear, longing, zeal and justice (vv. 8–12). Titus’s joy and Paul’s confidence in them complete his comfort (vv. 13–16). The chapter is one of Scripture’s best descriptions of true repentance.

Since we have these promises, beloved. Key words. The promises of 6:16–18: God dwelling among his people, being their God and Father.

Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit. Key words. “Cleanse” (katharizō). “Defilement” (molysmos, stain, pollution). Of body: sexual sin, idolatrous feasts. Of spirit: inner sins of pride, bitterness and false worship. Holiness covers the whole person. Notice “let us”: Paul includes himself.

Bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God. Key words. “Bringing to completion” (epiteleō, carrying through to the end). Holiness is a lifelong pursuit, motivated by reverent fear of God.

Where Christians differ: who does the cleansing? Some say sanctification is entirely God’s work, with believers passive; others say it is entirely up to our effort. Verdict: Paul calls believers to cleanse themselves, yet it is God who sanctifies by his Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Sanctification is God’s work in which we actively cooperate: we work out what God works in (Philippians 2:12–13; Westminster 13.1, 3). It is never complete in this life; perfect holiness comes at glorification.

What it does not mean. It does not mean we earn God’s promises by cleansing ourselves. We already have the promises; holiness is our response.

In a sentence. Since we have these promises, dear friends, let us purify ourselves from everything that contaminates body and spirit, perfecting holiness out of reverence for God.

On a Tuesday. Name one defilement of body or spirit in your life. Confess it, and take a practical step to clean it out today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–16 — Godly Grief, Worldly Grief, and Joy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul asks again for a place in their hearts, insisting he has wronged and exploited no one, and assuring them he says this in love, not accusation. He takes up the story from chapter 2: in Macedonia he had no rest, with conflict outside and fear inside, until God comforted him through Titus’s arrival and his news. The Corinthians had been grieved by the severe letter, and Paul briefly regretted sending it, but their grief led to repentance. He contrasts sorrow that turns to God and leads to salvation with worldly sorrow that leads to death, and lists the earnest, practical fruits their repentance produced. Titus was refreshed by them, Paul’s confidence in them proved justified, and he rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology: The distinction between godly grief and worldly grief is pastorally crucial. Worldly grief can look like repentance: tears, distress, self-accusation. But its focus is on the pain caused to oneself (loss of reputation, loss of relationships, loss of comfort) rather than on the offence against God. Judas displays worldly grief — he is distraught over what he has done, even returns the money, but cannot receive forgiveness; he destroys himself. Peter displays godly grief — the same tears, the same self-accusation, but directed toward the face of Jesus, resolved by Jesus’s restoration. The direction of the grief determines its outcome.
verseByVerse.examples: A pastor is confronted with evidence of long-term financial dishonesty. He weeps, expresses remorse, describes how devastated he is — by the damage to his reputation, the pain to his family, the end of his ministry. He never directly addresses the harm done to those he stole from, or the offence against God. His leadership team recognises, with the categories of this passage, that they are witnessing worldly grief — real grief, but pointed in the wrong direction. Genuine repentance would ask different questions: not “what have I lost?” but “against whom have I sinned, and what must I do to make it right?”

verseByVerse.quote: Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Make room in your hearts for us. We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. I do not say this to condemn you, for I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.

Make room in your hearts for us. Key words. “Make room” (chōreō, give space). Picking up 6:11–13.

We have wronged no one, we have corrupted no one, we have taken advantage of no one. Key words. Three denials, probably answering accusations. Wronged (adikeō, treated unjustly). Corrupted (phtheirō, ruined, led astray morally or doctrinally). Taken advantage (pleonekteō, exploited, cheated), perhaps a charge about the collection (12:17–18).

I do not say this to condemn you. Key words. He is not accusing them.

For I said before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together. Key words. A pledge of unbreakable loyalty, like friends who swore to live and die together. Paul’s love will not let go of them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was sinless. It means his conduct toward them had been honest.

In a sentence. Make room for us in your hearts. We have wronged no one, corrupted no one, exploited no one. Paul does not say this to condemn you; he has said before that you have such a place in our hearts that we would live or die with you.

For worship. Thank God for friends who are committed to you in life and death. Be that kind of friend.

verseByVerse.quote: I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am acting with great boldness toward you; I have great pride in you; I am filled with comfort. In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy.

I am acting with great boldness toward you. Key words. “Boldness” (parrēsia, frankness, confidence).

I have great pride in you. Key words. After all the trouble, Paul boasts of them.

I am filled with comfort. Key words. The theme of chapter 1 returns.

In all our affliction, I am overflowing with joy. Key words. “Overflowing” (hyperperisseuomai, super-abounding). Joy in the middle of affliction, not after it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean affliction ended. It means joy can overflow even in it.

In a sentence. Paul speaks to you with great frankness; he takes great pride in you. He is greatly encouraged; in all our troubles his joy knows no bounds.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone today that you are proud of them in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

For even when we came into Macedonia, our bodies had no rest. Key words. Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus. “Bodies” (literally flesh): his whole human self.

But we were afflicted at every turn—fighting without and fear within. Key words. Outward conflicts: opposition, perhaps persecution in Macedonia. Inward fears: anxiety for the Corinthians, and perhaps for Titus’s safety. Paul is honest about fear.

But God, who comforts the downcast. Key words. From Isaiah 49:13: God comforts his afflicted ones. “Downcast” (tapeinos, lowly, depressed). God is especially near the downhearted.

Comforted us by the coming of Titus. Key words. God’s comfort came through a person. God often comforts us through friends.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fear is always sin. Paul felt fear. Faith brings it to God.

In a sentence. For when we came into Macedonia, we had no rest, but were harassed at every turn: conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the coming of Titus,

For worship. If you are downcast, the God who comforts the downcast is near. Ask him to send you comfort, perhaps through a friend.
verseByVerse.note: Paul picks up the story he broke off in 2:13: waiting anxiously for Titus.

verseByVerse.quote: and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you, as he told us of your longing, your mourning, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.

And not only by his coming but also by the comfort with which he was comforted by you. Key words. Titus had been encouraged by the Corinthians’ response, and passed it on to Paul. Comfort flows around the body of Christ (1:4).

As he told us of your longing. Key words. They longed to see Paul again.

Your mourning. Key words. They grieved over the offence and over hurting him.

Your zeal for me. Key words. They were eager to defend him and put things right.

So that I rejoiced still more. Key words. Paul’s joy was even greater than his relief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all problems were solved. Chapters 10–13 show some opposition remained.

In a sentence. and not only by his coming but also by the comfort you had given him. He told us about your longing for us, your deep sorrow, your eager concern for Paul, so that Paul’s joy was greater than ever.

On a Tuesday. Pass on good news about other believers. It comforts and encourages.

verseByVerse.quote: For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For even if I made you grieve with my letter, I do not regret it—though I did regret it, for I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while.

For even if I made you grieve with my letter. Key words. The severe, tearful letter (2:3–4).

I do not regret it—though I did regret it. Key words. Honest about mixed feelings. After sending it, Paul worried whether he had been too harsh. Now he sees it was right.

For I see that that letter grieved you, though only for a while. Key words. The pain was real, but temporary, and led to good.

What it does not mean. It does not mean inspiration removes all human emotion. Paul felt doubts. God’s word came through a real person.

In a sentence. Even if Paul caused you sorrow by his letter, he does not regret it. Though he did regret it at first, he sees that the letter hurt you, but only for a little while,

For worship. If you have had to say something hard in love, leave the results with God.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. For you felt a godly grief, so that you suffered no loss through us. For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death.

As it is, I rejoice, not because you were grieved, but because you were grieved into repenting. Key words. Paul does not enjoy their pain. He rejoices in its fruit: repentance (metanoia, a change of mind and direction).

For you felt a godly grief. Key words. Literally, grief according to God: sorrow that God approves, that sees sin as God sees it.

So that you suffered no loss through us. Key words. The letter hurt, but did them only good.

For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret. Key words. Godly grief leads to repentance, which leads to salvation, and is never regretted. “Without regret” (ametamelētos): no one ever regrets true repentance.

Whereas worldly grief produces death. Key words. Worldly sorrow: regret over consequences, embarrassment, self-pity, being caught, without turning to God. It leads to despair, bitterness and death. Judas felt remorse and despaired (Matthew 27:3–5); Peter wept and was restored (Luke 22:62; John 21:15–19).

Godly and worldly grief. Godly grief is sorry for sin because it offends God; worldly grief is sorry for the consequences. Godly grief runs to God; worldly grief runs from him. Godly grief changes behaviour; worldly grief only feels bad. The Westminster Shorter Catechism defines repentance unto life as a sinner’s grief and hatred of sin, turning from it to God, with full purpose of new obedience (Q. 87).

What it does not mean. It does not mean repentance earns salvation. It is the fruit of grace and the way into salvation’s blessings.

In a sentence. Yet now Paul is happy, not because you were made sorry, but because your sorrow led you to repentance. For you became sorrowful as God intended and so were not harmed in any way by us. Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but worldly sorrow brings death.

For worship. Ask God for godly grief over your sin: not mere regret, but sorrow that turns you back to him.

parallels.desc: Peter’s tears and Judas’s remorse

verseByVerse.quote: For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you, but also what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what fear, what longing, what zeal, what punishment! At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter.

For see what earnestness this godly grief has produced in you. Key words. Seven marks of true repentance. Earnestness (spoudē): seriousness, no longer indifferent.

But also what eagerness to clear yourselves. Key words. Literally, defence (apologia): eagerness to put things right and show they did not approve of the wrong.

What indignation. Key words. Anger at the sin and at themselves for tolerating it.

What fear. Key words. Reverent fear of God, and perhaps of Paul’s discipline.

What longing. Key words. Longing for restored fellowship.

What zeal. Key words. Zeal for what is right, for Paul, for God’s honour.

What punishment! Key words. “Punishment” (ekdikēsis, justice, vindication): they disciplined the offender (2:6). Repentance acts to put wrongs right.

At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in the matter. Key words. “Innocent” (hagnos, pure, clear). By their response, they showed they were not complicit.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they were never at fault. It means their repentance cleared them.

In a sentence. See what this godly sorrow has produced in you: what earnestness, what eagerness to clear yourselves, what indignation, what alarm, what longing, what concern, what readiness to see justice done. At every point you have proved yourselves innocent in this matter.

On a Tuesday. Test your repentance by these marks. Is it earnest? Does it want to put things right? Does it act?

verseByVerse.quote: So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong, nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong, but in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God.

So although I wrote to you, it was not for the sake of the one who did the wrong. Key words. Not mainly to punish the offender.

Nor for the sake of the one who suffered the wrong. Key words. Not mainly to vindicate the one offended, probably Paul himself.

But in order that your earnestness for us might be revealed to you in the sight of God. Key words. The main purpose: that the Corinthians would discover, before God, how much they really did care about Paul and the truth. Sometimes we do not know our own hearts until tested.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the wrong did not matter. It means Paul’s deepest concern was the church’s spiritual health.

In a sentence. So even though Paul wrote to you, it was neither on account of the one who did the wrong nor on account of the injured party, but rather that before God you could see for yourselves how devoted to us you are.

For worship. Ask God to show you your own heart, and to make your love for him and his people sincere.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore we are comforted. And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true.

Therefore we are comforted. Key words. The outcome.

And besides our own comfort, we rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus. Key words. Paul delights in his friend’s happiness.

Because his spirit has been refreshed by you all. Key words. “Refreshed” (anapauō, rested). Titus went expecting trouble and found warmth.

For whatever boasts I made to him about you, I was not put to shame. Key words. Before sending Titus, Paul had told him good things about the Corinthians, perhaps to encourage him. They proved true.

But just as everything we said to you was true, so also our boasting before Titus has proved true. Key words. Paul’s word is reliable, whether to them or about them (1:18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul flattered them. He spoke the truth both ways.

In a sentence. By all this we are encouraged. In addition to our own encouragement, we were especially delighted to see how happy Titus was, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you. Paul had boasted to him about you, and you have not embarrassed him. Just as everything we said to you was true, so our boasting about you to Titus has proved true as well.

On a Tuesday. Speak well of other believers to others, and live in a way that makes others’ good words about you true.

verseByVerse.quote: And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his affection for you is even greater, as he remembers the obedience of you all, how you received him with fear and trembling. I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you.

And his affection for you is even greater. Key words. “Affection” (splanchna, deep inner feelings). Titus loves them more now.

As he remembers the obedience of you all. Key words. They obeyed the apostolic instructions.

How you received him with fear and trembling. Key words. With reverence and humility, taking his message seriously as from God (Philippians 2:12; Ephesians 6:5).

I rejoice, because I have complete confidence in you. Key words. “Complete confidence” (tharreō en panti, take courage in everything). This prepares for his appeal about the collection in chapters 8–9.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul thought them perfect. Chapters 10–13 show remaining concerns. But he rejoices in their present response.

In a sentence. And his affection for you is all the greater when he remembers that you were all obedient, receiving him with fear and trembling. Paul is glad he can have complete confidence in you.

For worship. Receive God’s word, and those who bring it, with humble reverence. Thank God for faithful messengers.
