8.title: The Grace of Giving: Christ Became Poor
8.overview:
Chapters 8 and 9 are about money: the collection Paul was gathering from his Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem. Some background helps. The Jerusalem church had been poor for years. There was a famine under the emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28–30), many believers had lost work or family support for following Jesus, and the church had many widows (Acts 6:1). When Paul’s apostleship was recognised in Jerusalem, the leaders asked him to “remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do” (Galatians 2:10). For Paul the collection was more than relief. It was a sign that Jews and Gentiles were one body: the Gentiles, who had shared in Israel’s spiritual blessings, were sharing material blessings in return (Romans 15:25–27). Corinth had started eagerly a year earlier (1 Corinthians 16:1–4), but the quarrel with Paul had stalled it.

In chapter 8 Paul encourages them to finish. He points to the poor, persecuted churches of Macedonia, who gave beyond their means and begged to take part, because they first gave themselves to the Lord. Above all he points to Christ, who though he was rich became poor for our sake, so that we might become rich. Giving should be willing, proportionate to what one has, and aimed at fairness between churches. Then Paul introduces the team who will collect the money, Titus and two trusted brothers, chosen so that the handling of the gift will be above suspicion before God and people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Macedonian Example and Christ Who Became Poor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul turns to the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. He describes the Macedonian churches, who in severe trials and deep poverty gave joyfully and beyond their means, even begging to be allowed to take part, because they had first given themselves to the Lord. He urges the Corinthians, who excel in so much, to excel in this generosity too. It is not a command; it is a test of genuine love, measured against the example of Christ, who was rich yet became poor for their sake so that they might become rich. They began a year ago; now they should finish, giving in proportion to what they have. The aim is not to burden them but fairness between churches, as with the manna in the wilderness, where no one had too much or too little.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is one of the key NT texts for the kenosis of the incarnation (alongside Phil. 2:5–8 and John 1:1–14). “Though he was rich” describes the pre-incarnate state of the Son — possessing all the resources of divine glory, honour, and power. “He became poor” describes the incarnation and more specifically the cross: the Son laid aside the exercise of divine prerogatives and took on the condition of creaturely poverty, ultimately the poverty of crucifixion and cursed death. “That you by his poverty might become rich” — the result is the enrichment of believers: forgiveness, adoption, the Spirit, the inheritance of the new creation.
verseByVerse.examples: A church board is considering its annual budget and the portion allocated to mission outside its own walls. One member argues that they should ensure their own facilities and staff are well-funded before giving generously abroad. This passage holds before him the Macedonian model: churches in deep poverty begging to give. And the Christological ground: the Son of God did not ensure his own comfort before giving to others. The board’s question is not merely financial but spiritual: does this budget reflect the grace described in v. 9?

verseByVerse.quote: We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia, for in a severe test of affliction, their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part.

Meaning first. Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem, which the Corinthians had begun a year earlier but not finished (1 Corinthians 16:1–4). These two chapters are the Bible’s fullest teaching on Christian giving. Chapter 8 makes three points. First, the example of the Macedonian churches, who, though desperately poor and afflicted, begged to give, beyond their means, because they first gave themselves to the Lord (vv. 1–5). Second, the supreme example and motive: the grace of the Lord Jesus, who though rich became poor so that we might become rich (vv. 6–9). Third, practical principles: finish what you started; giving is measured by willingness, not amount; and the goal is fairness, so that abundance meets need, as with the manna in the wilderness (vv. 10–15). Then Paul commends Titus and two trusted brothers who will handle the collection, so that everything is done honourably in the sight of God and people (vv. 16–24). Notice that Paul never uses the word money in these chapters; he calls the gift grace, fellowship, service, blessing and generosity.

We want you to know, brothers, about the grace of God that has been given among the churches of Macedonia. Key words. Macedonia: northern Greece, with churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. “Grace” (charis): generosity is a gift of God’s grace at work. The word appears ten times in chapters 8–9.

For in a severe test of affliction. Key words. The Macedonian churches faced persecution from the start (Acts 16:19–24; 17:5–9; 1 Thessalonians 1:6; 2:14).

Their abundance of joy and their extreme poverty. Key words. “Extreme poverty” (literally poverty down to the depths). Yet they had abundant joy. Joy and poverty together produced generosity.

Have overflowed in a wealth of generosity on their part. Key words. “Generosity” (haplotēs, simplicity, single-heartedness, liberality). Giving without calculating or holding back.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only the poor can be truly generous. It means generosity comes from grace and joy, not from having plenty.

In a sentence. And now, brothers and sisters, we want you to know about the grace God has given the Macedonian churches. In the middle of a very severe trial, their overflowing joy and their extreme poverty welled up in rich generosity.

On a Tuesday. You do not need to be rich to be generous. Give out of joy in God, whatever you have.
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 8–9 concern the collection for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The Macedonian churches — Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — were poor and persecuted.

verseByVerse.quote: For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—
verseByVerse.commentary:
For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means, of their own accord, begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints—

For they gave according to their means, as I can testify, and beyond their means. Key words. They gave what they could, and then more than seemed possible. Sacrificial giving, like the widow’s two coins (Mark 12:41–44).

Of their own accord. Key words. “Of their own accord” (authairetoi, self-chosen, voluntary). No pressure was needed.

Begging us earnestly for the favor of taking part in the relief of the saints. Key words. Astonishing: they begged to be allowed to give. Paul may have hesitated to ask such poor churches. “Favour” (charis, grace, privilege). “Taking part” (koinōnia, fellowship, partnership). “Relief” (diakonia, service, ministry). Giving is a privilege of partnership, not a burden.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should give irresponsibly, neglecting their families (1 Timothy 5:8). It means giving should be generous and joyful.

In a sentence. For Paul testifies that they gave as much as they were able, and even beyond their ability. Entirely on their own, they urgently pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the Lord’s people.

For worship. See giving as a privilege. Thank God for the chance to share in what he is doing.

parallels.desc: the widow gave out of her poverty

verseByVerse.quote: and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and this, not as we expected, but they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us.

And this, not as we expected. Key words. Their response exceeded all expectations.

But they gave themselves first to the Lord. Key words. The secret of their generosity. Before giving money, they gave themselves. When the heart belongs to the Lord, the wallet follows. Giving begins with consecration (Romans 12:1).

And then by the will of God to us. Key words. Then they gave themselves to Paul and his mission, as God willed.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving money can replace giving yourself. God wants you first, and then your gifts.

In a sentence. And they went beyond what we expected: they gave themselves first of all to the Lord, and then, by the will of God, to us as well.

On a Tuesday. Before you decide what to give, give yourself again to the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started, so he should complete among you this act of grace.

Accordingly, we urged Titus that as he had started. Key words. Titus had begun organising the collection in Corinth, perhaps on an earlier visit.

So he should complete among you this act of grace. Key words. “Act of grace” (charis): giving is grace in action. “Complete” (epiteleō, finish, as in 7:1).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Titus would pressure them. He would help them complete what they wanted to do.

In a sentence. So we urged Titus, just as he had made a beginning earlier, to bring this act of grace on your part to completion.

For worship. Pray for those in your church who organise giving and generosity. Thank God for them.

verseByVerse.quote: But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as you excel in everything—in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you—see that you excel in this act of grace also.

But as you excel in everything. Key words. “Excel” (perisseuō, abound). The Corinthians were richly gifted (1 Corinthians 1:5–7).

In faith, in speech, in knowledge, in all earnestness, and in our love for you. Key words. Their gifts and their recent earnest repentance (7:11). Some manuscripts read your love for us; the ESV notes this.

See that you excel in this act of grace also. Key words. Generosity is a grace to excel in, as much as faith or knowledge. A church rich in spiritual gifts should also be rich in giving.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is more important than faith. It means it is part of a complete Christian life.

In a sentence. But since you excel in everything, in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in complete earnestness and in the love we have kindled in you, see that you also excel in this grace of giving.

On a Tuesday. If you are strong in knowledge and faith, ask: am I also strong in generosity?

verseByVerse.quote: I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this not as a command, but to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine.

I say this not as a command. Key words. Paul does not order them to give. Christian giving must be voluntary (9:7).

But to prove by the earnestness of others that your love also is genuine. Key words. “Prove” (dokimazō, test). The Macedonians’ example tests the Corinthians’ love. Genuine love gives (1 John 3:17–18).

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving is optional for Christians. It means it must be willing, not forced.

In a sentence. Paul is not commanding you, but testing the sincerity of your love by comparing it with the earnestness of others.

For worship. Let your giving be a test you are glad to pass: a proof of genuine love.

verseByVerse.quote: For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.

For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The supreme motive for giving: Christ’s grace. You know it: you have experienced it.

That though he was rich. Key words. Rich in the glory he shared with the Father before the world began (John 17:5; Philippians 2:6). He owned everything.

Yet for your sake he became poor. Key words. The incarnation and the cross. He laid aside the privileges of glory, was born in a stable, had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58), and died stripped naked on a cross. “Became poor” (ptōcheuō, became a beggar).

So that you by his poverty might become rich. Key words. Rich in salvation: forgiveness, righteousness, adoption, the Spirit, eternal life, an inheritance (Ephesians 1:3, 18). A great exchange, like 5:21.

Where Christians differ: what did the Son give up? Some (kenotic theories) teach that the Son gave up some of his divine attributes, such as omniscience, when he became man. Verdict: The Son did not stop being God or lose any divine attribute. He became poor by taking a human nature and the humble life and death of a servant, veiling his glory and not using his divine privileges for himself (Philippians 2:6–8). He remained fully God while becoming fully man (Chalcedonian Definition; Westminster 8.2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s poverty promises believers material wealth. The riches are spiritual and eternal, as the prosperity gospel forgets.

In a sentence. For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ: though he was rich, for your sake he became poor, so that through his poverty you might become rich.

For worship. Meditate on Christ, rich, becoming poor for you. Then give, in gratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in this matter I give my judgment: this benefits you, who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have.

And in this matter I give my judgment. Key words. Advice, not command (v. 8).

This benefits you. Key words. Giving is good for the giver: it frees from greed and grows the soul (Acts 20:35).

Who a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. Key words. The Corinthians were the first to begin, and to want to (1 Corinthians 16:1–2). But they had stalled, perhaps because of the troubles.

So now finish doing it as well. Key words. Good intentions must become action.

So that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have. Key words. Out of what you have: according to your means. Not beyond what you possess.

What it does not mean. It does not mean they had failed completely. It means they needed to follow through.

In a sentence. Here is Paul’s judgement about what is best for you: last year you were the first not only to give but also to want to give. Now finish the work, so that your eager willingness may be matched by your completion of it, according to your means.

On a Tuesday. Is there a generous intention you have not followed through on? Finish it this week.

verseByVerse.quote: For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have.

For if the readiness is there. Key words. “Readiness” (prothymia, eagerness, willingness). God looks first at the heart.

It is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have. Key words. God measures the gift by what the giver has. A small gift from little is as acceptable as a large gift from much (Mark 12:43–44). No one is expected to give what they do not have.

What it does not mean. It does not mean willingness is enough without action. Paul has just said: finish it. It means God does not demand the impossible.

In a sentence. For if the willingness is there, the gift is acceptable according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.

For worship. Thank God that he looks at the heart, and accepts the willing gift of the poor as gladly as the rich.

verseByVerse.quote: For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened, but that as a matter of fairness your abundance at the present time should supply their need, so that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness.

For I do not mean that others should be eased and you burdened. Key words. Paul is not asking the Corinthians to impoverish themselves for others’ comfort.

But that as a matter of fairness. Key words. “Fairness” (isotēs, equality, balance). The aim is that no believer lacks the necessities while others have plenty.

Your abundance at the present time should supply their need. Key words. Corinth had more; Jerusalem had less. Now the Corinthians share.

So that their abundance may supply your need, that there may be fairness. Key words. Circumstances change; one day the Corinthians may be in need, and others will help them. The church is a family that shares.

Where Christians differ: Christian sharing and economics. Some use this passage to support enforced redistribution of wealth by the state. Others ignore it. Verdict: Paul is speaking of voluntary giving within the body of Christ, not compulsory state action (v. 8; 9:7). He does not call for absolute equality of possessions, but for generous sharing so that no believer lacks basic needs. Christians remain owners of their goods as stewards, but are called to deep generosity, especially to fellow believers (Acts 4:32–35; Galatians 6:10; 1 John 3:17). Christians may disagree on public policy, but they cannot neglect personal generosity.

What it does not mean. It does not mean wealth is evil or that all Christians must have exactly the same. It means abundance carries responsibility.

In a sentence. Our desire is not that others might be relieved while you are hard pressed, but that there might be fairness. At the present time your plenty will supply what they need, so that in turn their plenty will supply what you need. The goal is fairness.

On a Tuesday. Look at your abundance. Whose need could it meet? Share it.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.”

As it is written, “Whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.” Key words. From Exodus 16:18, about the manna in the wilderness. Some gathered more, some less, but when measured, everyone had enough. Hoarding was pointless, since extra manna rotted (Exodus 16:20). God provided for all. Paul applies this to the church: through generous sharing, God’s provision reaches everyone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean there will be no differences in wealth. It means that in God’s family, no one should be left in need.

In a sentence. As it is written: “The one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little.”

For worship. Thank God for his daily provision. Trust him enough to share, rather than hoard.

parallels.desc: whoever gathered much had nothing left over

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–24 — Titus and the Brothers; Transparency in Giving
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul thanks God for Titus’s eagerness to return to Corinth and introduces two companions: a brother well known among the churches for his gospel work and chosen by the churches to travel with the gift, and another brother proven in many tests. The arrangement is deliberate. Paul wants the handling of the money to be honourable not only before the Lord but in the eyes of people, so that no one can accuse him. He commends these representatives of the churches and asks the Corinthians to show them openly the love that Paul has boasted of.
verseByVerse.theology: The principle of handling ministry finances with transparent accountability applies directly to all Christian organisations. Paul, who could have simply trusted his own integrity, insists on multiple overseers and transparent processes — because the integrity of the ministry is at stake not only in God’s sight but in the sight of the watching world. Financial scandal in Christian ministry has consistently damaged the gospel’s credibility; Paul’s precaution (v. 20) is prophylactic wisdom.
verseByVerse.examples: A mission organisation implements a new policy requiring two-signature approval for all expenditures over a certain threshold, and annual independent financial audits reported to the whole organisation. Some staff feel this implies distrust. This passage gives the theological rationale: the precautions are not about distrust of individuals but about protecting the honour of the Lord and the integrity of the ministry in the sight of those who would use any irregularity to attack the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. For he not only accepted our appeal, but being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord.

But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you. Key words. God gave Titus a love for the Corinthians like Paul’s. Good desires in our hearts come from God (Philippians 2:13).

For he not only accepted our appeal. Key words. Paul asked him to go.

But being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord. Key words. He wanted to go anyway. God’s will and his own desire coincided.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Titus had no choice. God worked in his heart, and he freely chose.

In a sentence. Thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same concern Paul has for you. For Titus not only welcomed our appeal, but he is coming to you with much enthusiasm and on his own initiative.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for the good desires he puts in your heart. Act on them.

verseByVerse.quote: With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will.

With him we are sending the brother who is famous among all the churches for his preaching of the gospel. Key words. The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke, others Barnabas, Silas or Apollos. His fame was for gospel ministry.

And not only that, but he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us. Key words. “Appointed” (cheirotoneō, elected, chosen by show of hands). The churches chose him as their representative.

As we carry out this act of grace that is being ministered by us. Key words. The collection.

For the glory of the Lord himself and to show our good will. Key words. The collection glorifies Christ and shows the eagerness of all involved.

What it does not mean. It does not mean his name is important for us to know. God knows him; that is enough.

In a sentence. And we are sending along with him the brother who is praised by all the churches for his service to the gospel. What is more, he was chosen by the churches to accompany us as we carry this gift, which we administer to honour the Lord himself and to show our eagerness to help.

For worship. Thank God for unnamed, faithful servants of the gospel. Most of God’s best workers are unknown to history.
verseByVerse.note: The famous brother is unnamed; some early writers guessed Luke.

verseByVerse.quote: We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us, for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man.

We take this course so that no one should blame us about this generous gift that is being administered by us. Key words. Paul’s critics might accuse him of stealing from the collection (12:16–18). So he has independent, church-appointed people travel with the money.

For we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord’s sight but also in the sight of man. Key words. From Proverbs 3:4 in the Greek. It is not enough to be honest before God; we must also be seen to be honest. Financial accountability protects both the gospel and the ministers.

What it does not mean. It does not mean reputation matters more than integrity. Integrity comes first, and transparency shows it.

In a sentence. We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift. For we are taking pains to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord but also in the eyes of people.

On a Tuesday. In handling money, at church or work, be transparent. Make it easy for others to see you are honest.

verseByVerse.quote: And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters, but who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ.

And with them we are sending our brother whom we have often tested and found earnest in many matters. Key words. A third person, proven in faithfulness.

But who is now more earnest than ever because of his great confidence in you. Key words. He believes in the Corinthians.

As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker for your benefit. Key words. Partner (koinōnos) and fellow worker (synergos).

And as for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches. Key words. The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles”: men sent by the churches as their delegates. Not apostles of Christ like the Twelve and Paul, but representatives sent on a mission.

The glory of Christ. Key words. Such faithful servants bring honour to Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean these men held the apostolic office. The word is used in its general sense, sent ones.

In a sentence. In addition, we are sending with them our brother who has often proved to us in many ways that he is zealous, and now even more so because of his great confidence in you. As for Titus, he is Paul’s partner and co-worker among you; as for our brothers, they are representatives of the churches and an honour to Christ.

For worship. Thank God for faithful co-workers in his kingdom. Be one yourself.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “messengers” is literally “apostles” — men sent by the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So give proof before the churches of your love and of our boasting about you to these men.

So give proof before the churches of your love. Key words. Show these representatives, and through them all the churches, that your love is real.

And of our boasting about you to these men. Key words. Paul has praised the Corinthians to others. Let your actions confirm it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean giving for show. It means letting genuine love be seen.

In a sentence. Therefore show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our pride in you, so that the churches can see it.

On a Tuesday. Let your love be visible in action, especially in welcoming and supporting those who serve.
