13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The letter ends with a warning and a blessing. Paul is about to make his third visit, and he will deal with unrepented sin properly, on the evidence of witnesses, as the law requires. The Corinthians have demanded proof that Christ speaks through him; they will have it. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will live with him by God’s power in dealing with them. But the real test is theirs: they must examine themselves to see whether they are in the faith, whether Christ is in them. Paul would rather appear to fail than see them do wrong; his authority is for building up, not tearing down, and he writes now so that he will not need to be severe when he arrives.

Then the tone softens into final appeals: rejoice, aim for restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. After greetings, the letter closes with the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. The letter that began with the God of all comfort ends with the triune God present with a troubled church.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul announces his third visit. Any charge will be settled by two or three witnesses, and he warns those who sinned before, and everyone else, that this time he will not spare them. They wanted evidence that Christ speaks through him: Christ is not weak towards them but powerful among them. He was crucified in weakness yet lives by God’s power, and his servants, weak in him, will live with him by that same power in their dealings with the church. Paul turns the test round: they should examine themselves to see whether they are really in the faith, and recognise that Christ is in them, unless they fail the test. He hopes they will see that he has not failed. His prayer is that they do no wrong, not so that he looks good, but so that they do right even if he seems to have failed. He can do nothing against the truth, only for it. He is glad to be weak if they are strong, and prays for their restoration. That is why he writes before coming: so that he will not have to use his authority harshly, since the Lord gave it to him to build up, not to tear down.
verseByVerse.theology: The call to self-examination (v. 5) has been used in Reformed tradition as the basis for the practice of self-examination before the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11:28–31). Genuine self-examination is not the cultivation of paralyzing doubt but the honest assessment of the soul before God: am I in the faith? Is Christ in me? Is my trust in Christ or in my own religious performance? The examination that produces assurance is the examination that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the examination that finds sufficient personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prepares for a communion service and the pastor leads a five-minute self-examination period before the elements are distributed. Some members treat it as a routine; others spiral into anxiety. This passage clarifies the goal: not to find sufficient personal holiness to “qualify” for the table, but to find whether Christ is there — whether the faith that receives him is genuine. The person who comes to the table trusting Christ is examining themselves correctly; the person who comes evaluating their performance has missed the point of both the examination and the table.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—

Meaning first. 2 Corinthians 13 closes the letter with a final warning and a final blessing. First, Paul announces his third visit. He will act with justice, establishing every charge by witnesses, and will not spare the unrepentant. The Corinthians want proof that Christ speaks through him; they will get it. Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God’s power, and Paul, weak in him, will deal with them by that power (vv. 1–4). Second, he turns the test around: examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Paul hopes they will pass, and prays that they will do right, even if he seems weak, because his authority is for building up, not tearing down (vv. 5–10). Finally, he gives brief commands: rejoice, aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree, live in peace. He sends greetings, and ends with the fullest Trinitarian blessing in the New Testament: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit (vv. 11–14).

This is the third time I am coming to you. Key words. After the founding visit and the painful visit (2:1).

Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. Key words. From Deuteronomy 19:15, also Jesus’ rule for church discipline (Matthew 18:16) and for accusations against elders (1 Timothy 5:19). Paul will not act on rumour. Due process and justice in the church.

I warned those who sinned before and all the others. Key words. He warned them on the second visit.

And I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them. Key words. A clear final warning. He will exercise discipline.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul is eager to punish. He has given many warnings and much time.

In a sentence. This will be Paul’s third visit to you. Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses. He already gave you a warning when he was with you the second time. He now repeats it while absent: on his return he will not spare those who sinned earlier or any of the others,

On a Tuesday. Never act on rumour against a fellow believer. Insist on clear evidence and fair process.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three

verseByVerse.quote: since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

Since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. Key words. “Proof” (dokimē, test result). The Corinthians demanded evidence that Paul really spoke for Christ.

He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you. Key words. Christ himself has shown his power among them: in their conversion, the gifts, the miracles. They should not doubt Christ’s power in Paul’s ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christ’s power is always visible as human strength. It is often displayed through weakness (12:9).

In a sentence. since you are demanding proof that Christ is speaking through Paul. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

For worship. Thank Christ for his power at work in your church, often in quiet ways.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.

For he was crucified in weakness. Key words. The cross looked like utter weakness (1 Corinthians 1:25). Christ chose weakness.

But lives by the power of God. Key words. The resurrection displayed God’s power (Romans 1:4; Ephesians 1:19–20).

For we also are weak in him. Key words. Paul shares Christ’s weakness, in suffering and humility.

But in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God. Key words. And he shares Christ’s resurrection power, which will be seen when he comes to deal with them. The pattern of cross and resurrection shapes all Christian ministry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean weakness and power are opposites to choose between. In Christ, they go together.

In a sentence. For to be sure, he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by God’s power. Likewise, we are weak in him, yet by God’s power we will live with him in our dealing with you.

On a Tuesday. Your weakness is not the end of the story. In Christ, resurrection power follows.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!

Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Key words. The Corinthians were testing Paul. He turns it around. “Examine” (peirazō, test, put to the proof). “In the faith”: truly believing, united to Christ.

Test yourselves. Key words. “Test” (dokimazō, prove, as metal is tested).

Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? Key words. The sign of a true believer: Christ dwells in them by his Spirit (Romans 8:9–10; Galatians 2:20; Colossians 1:27).

Unless indeed you fail to meet the test! Key words. “Fail the test” (adokimos, disqualified, counterfeit). If they find Christ is in them, then their faith came through Paul, which proves his apostleship. If not, they have bigger problems than Paul.

Where Christians differ: self-examination and assurance. Some say believers should never doubt their salvation; others make constant introspection the mark of true faith. Verdict: Self-examination is commanded, especially for those whose lives contradict their profession. Assurance rests first on God’s promises in Christ, confirmed by the inner witness of the Spirit and the fruit of a changed life (1 John; Westminster 18.2). Self-examination should lead not to endless morbid introspection but to looking at Christ, and to repentance where needed. Those who find Christ in them can rest assured.

What it does not mean. It does not mean salvation depends on perfect performance. It means real faith shows itself, and should be checked.

In a sentence. Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Do you not realise that Christ Jesus is in you, unless, of course, you fail the test?

For worship. Take time to examine yourself before God. Is Christ in you? If so, rest in him. If not, come to him now.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.

I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. Key words. Paul hopes they will see that he is genuine.

But we pray to God that you may not do wrong. Key words. His real concern: their holiness, not his reputation.

Not that we may appear to have met the test. Key words. He is not praying for his own vindication.

But that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed. Key words. If they repent and do right, Paul will have no need to show his authority in discipline, and may look weak again. He is happy with that, as long as they do right. Selfless love.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about the truth of his apostleship. He cared more about their good.

In a sentence. And Paul trusts that you will discover that we have not failed the test. Now we pray to God that you will not do anything wrong, not so that people will see that we have stood the test, but so that you will do what is right even though we may seem to have failed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for others’ holiness, even if it means you look less impressive.

verseByVerse.quote: For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth. Key words. The truth: the gospel and God’s will. Paul’s authority can only be used in the service of truth. If they are doing right, he has no grounds to discipline them. Church authority has limits: it cannot act against God’s truth.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul could not sin. It means apostolic authority was given only to serve the truth.

In a sentence. For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

For worship. Ask God to make you someone who always stands for the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.

For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Key words. Paul rejoices if he appears weak because they are strong in faith and holiness. Their strength is his joy.

Your restoration is what we pray for. Key words. “Restoration” (katartisis, being put right, mended, equipped, as nets are mended). Paul prays for the church to be made whole again.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul wanted to be weak for its own sake. He wanted them strong.

In a sentence. We are glad whenever we are weak but you are strong; and our prayer is that you may be fully restored.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s restoration and strength, even above your own reputation.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.

For this reason I write these things while I am away from you. Key words. The purpose of the letter.

That when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority. Key words. “Severe” (apotomōs, sharply, cuttingly). He writes now to avoid severity later.

That the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down. Key words. Repeated from 10:8. The Lord gave the authority, and its purpose is construction, not destruction. Echoes Jeremiah 1:10 and 24:6.

What it does not mean. It does not mean authority never corrects. Sometimes building up requires tearing down what is false.

In a sentence. This is why Paul writes these things when he is absent, that when he comes he may not have to be harsh in his use of authority, the authority the Lord gave him for building you up, not for tearing you down.

For worship. Thank God for leaders who correct in order to build up. Respond to correction quickly.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with brief appeals: rejoice, put things right, encourage one another, think alike, and live at peace, and the God of love and peace will be with them. They are to greet one another with a holy kiss, and he passes on greetings from all the believers with him. The final words are a blessing naming the Lord Jesus Christ, God the Father and the Holy Spirit together: may the grace of the Lord Jesus, the love of God and the fellowship of the Spirit be with them all.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction is not a formula but a theology: it presents the three persons in distinct but coordinated action, each contributing uniquely to the believer’s life. The order (Christ, Father, Spirit) is unusual — the more common Pauline order puts the Father first — possibly because the letter’s concerns have centred on the grace of Christ (the atonement of ch. 5, the self-giving of ch. 8). The coordinated action of all three persons in the single benediction is an implicit trinitarian claim: to receive grace, love, and fellowship from these three distinct persons is to receive from one God in three persons.

Koinōnia of the Holy Spirit — three possible meanings, all theologically valid: (1) the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers; (2) participation in the Spirit — sharing in the Spirit’s life; (3) the Spirit as the one who communicates fellowship with the Father and Son. These are not mutually exclusive; the Spirit’s work achieves all three simultaneously. Those who are indwelt by the Spirit share in the divine koinōnia — the mutual love and life of the Trinity — and that sharing is expressed in genuine community with one another.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that closes every service with this benediction has been pronouncing it for decades as a familiar liturgical ending. A new pastor stops before pronouncing it and asks the congregation: do you know what you are about to receive? Each phrase is unpacked slowly — the grace that flows from Christ’s cross, the love that originated in the Father’s heart before creation, the fellowship that the Spirit creates both with God and among the gathered community. The familiar words suddenly land with the weight they have always carried. The benediction is not a farewell; it is a sending into the world with the fullness of the Triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.

Finally, brothers, rejoice. Key words. “Rejoice” (chairō): this can also mean farewell, as a greeting. Both fit: goodbye, and be glad in the Lord.

Aim for restoration. Key words. “Restoration” (katartizō, be mended, as in v. 9). Work toward putting things right.

Comfort one another. Key words. Or: listen to my appeal. Either way, encouragement (parakaleō), the theme of chapter 1.

Agree with one another. Key words. Literally, think the same thing: be of one mind (Philippians 2:2).

Live in peace. Key words. End the quarrels (12:20).

And the God of love and peace will be with you. Key words. The only time this title, God of love and peace, appears in the New Testament. As they live in love and peace, they will know the God who is love and peace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God’s presence is earned. It means a church living in peace experiences his presence.

In a sentence. Finally, brothers and sisters, rejoice! Strive for full restoration, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you.

On a Tuesday. Pick one of these commands and do it today: rejoice, mend a relationship, encourage someone, agree, make peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. Key words. A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends in that culture. In the church, it expressed love, reconciliation and family belonging (Romans 16:16; 1 Corinthians 16:20). After all the conflict, a pointed command.

All the saints greet you. Key words. The believers with Paul in Macedonia. The wider church cares about them.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a literal kiss is required in every culture. It means warm, pure, family affection.

In a sentence. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All God’s people here send their greetings.

For worship. Greet your fellow believers warmly this Sunday, especially anyone you have been at odds with.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Key words. The free, undeserved favour shown in Christ, who though rich became poor for us (8:9). Grace comes first, because it is through Christ that we come to know the Father’s love.

And the love of God. Key words. The Father’s love, the source of everything (John 3:16; Romans 5:8).

And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Key words. “Fellowship” (koinōnia): sharing, communion. Either our fellowship with the Spirit, or the fellowship among believers that the Spirit creates. Both are true.

Be with you all. Key words. All: including those who opposed Paul. The letter ends with blessing for everyone.

The Trinity. This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is one of the clearest witnesses to the Trinity in Scripture. Each person is distinct, each gives a distinct blessing, and they are named side by side as equal sources of divine blessing. Written about twenty-five years after the resurrection, it shows that the early church worshipped one God in three persons. It has been used as a benediction in Christian worship ever since.

What it does not mean. It does not mean each blessing belongs to one person only. Grace, love and fellowship come from the one God. But each is especially associated with one person.

In a sentence. May the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

For worship. Pray this blessing over yourself, your family and your church today.
verseByVerse.note: This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is still widely used to close Christian worship.
